Mr. James Plant, who has just died at Leicester, at the age of 74, was a geologist of .more than local reputation, and was an active member of the Com- mittee of the British Association,which was formed for the collection of information ,concerning "the erratic rocks " or boulders of Great Britian. Beginn- ing life as a hosier, us scientific attainments soon brought him into prominence, and after a time he disposed of his business and became a consulting geologist, in which .capacity he acquired a lucrative connection.

-- A curious storris told of his brother, Mr. Nathan- iel Plant, who was a naturalist and travelled much in South America in search of rare fauna. Before he left this 'country the ,Leiceater Literary and Philosophical .Society 'presented him with a pa- tentous,looking testimonial engrossed on parch- ment, and with large 'red, efficial-looking 'seal attached. They Ihopild t anight be ot service to him in his travela, andpso it was in a most .uvez- pected way. • For ilm. One ,of the periodical out- breaks la South America .lie was taken prisoner, and actually sentenced to death. in the hour of tribulation, however, he bethought himself of is testimonial, produced it from the tin case in which he carried it, and so impressed the authorities with' his qualities that he was reapited and eventwilly released..

Mr.Jas. Alawdsley,the secretary of .tle Amalgam- ated Association of Operative Spisatiora, is A great character in his way, and is well-known to most of the " masters," who,apart from his oci&I position, have no small admiration for him, and hike to have ; a " crack " with him. Few men know the posi- tion of things, and the condition of trade., in Lau- cashire better than he does. Manufacturers are aware of that, and are not averse to taking his opinion thereon. Some of them, indeed, would not be borry if he would take their affairs in hand as he is now taking those of the operatives, feeling sure that he would pull them through.

But Mr. Mawdsley is true to his class, and is not likely to desert them. He formerly worked as an operative spinner for thirty shillings a week, and so knows exactly what the workmen want, knows also, as they believe, how to get it. But even while reMaining true to the operatives, he could aid the masters greatly if bey would allow him, for "Jim" as they call him, irno7,'!' tllOrcligt,ily that employers and employed alike are sufferiiig :from the same cause, and that together they could win, w.ne,..4118 divided they may have to suffer more and more. Ri)

-- Mr. Macdonald Cameron, whom Lord ipon has just appointed deputy master of the Sydney Mint, .bas many friends in Australia, for he is a much- 'travelled man. He began life in the Civil Service, but soon left the Government post he held to take part in a chemical business—his strong point being his scientific knowledge of chemistry. In the middle of last year he arrived from an exploring tour of many months in Borneo in time to be ousted from the representation of Wick Burghs by Sir John. Ptlnder. His new appointment is worth .£l,lOO. slrear.

Dr. Nansen did not address the Geographical Society for the first time last night. When he returned from his Greenland trip he read a paper before the society. He has a capital presence, and without being actually eloquent he is a really en- gaging speaker. He knows English so perfectly that it is only now and then his slight foreign accent betrays itself. Dr. Nanseu does not expect to be in this country again previous to sailing from Norway iti search of the North Pole. Between his return in a few days to Norway, and his departure in Jt1.145 he will be engaged in superintending preparations for hi c expedition.

Sir John Mowbray is to resign his post of Church Estate Commissioner, with its attendant salary of £l,OOO a year. Sir John has an unbroken Parlia- mentary record since 1853, a term of service: Bur- 'l passed only by Mr. Gladstone,Mr. "Thera, andl ; until the last election by Sir Rainafd Kniubtleki of Fawsley. Like Sir John Clorst, the retiring Church Estate Commissioner has changed his namet He began life as Cornish. Sir John became a Privy Councillor in 1868. Few men are more popular in the House of Commons than this cheerful-looking old gentleman, whose abandonment of his duties as a Commissioner probably preludes his retire- ment from public life altogether.

An engagement of considerable interest will he shortly announced between the Cesarevitch of Russia. Ataman of all the Cossacks, &c., and Prin- cess Marie of Greece, who since the death of let , sister Princess Alexandra (Grand Duchess Paul of I Russia), is the eldest daughter of the King and Queen of Greece. There have been very consider- able difficulties to be smoothed away, for, apart ' from the fact that the Princess will not be seven- teen till February, and that the Cesarevitch's antemic condition renders him a very unsuitable subject for matrimony, the Greek Church prohibits marriages between first cousins. The Czar, how- ever, is the head of his own Church, and an do as he pleases—which is a very happy condition. The marriage is. moreover, such an obviously advanta- geous one for Greece that the ecclesiastics of the hitter country have given way, and a joint dispen- sation will be issued.

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1892.
1.0.0. T. NO. 1. CON VENTION, S.W. LANCASHIRE.

This Convention held its quarterly session on Saturday, in the Baptist Schoolroom; Deacon-road, Widnes. Bro. Morris Jones, D.C.T., presided. The Secretary (Bro. Richard Kean,W arrington) reported an increase of 48 members during the quarter. The following lodges, Walter Bonehill, St. Helens Ebenezer, Hope of Hindley, Temperance Mission, Hope of Earles- town, Young 40th, and Hope of Wigan, had each ' in- creased their membership,special note being made of the Walter Bonehill, whose membership had increased froma 12 last quarter to 34 this. The Hope of Earlestown also had made grand progress, viz.,from 29 to 48. The Hope .of Wigan had opened a Senior Temple during the quar- ter, and also increased six in their subordinate lodge. In Warrington, Earlestown, and St. Helens. Saturday evening concerts bad been commenced as a counter-attraction to the public house. and had so far proved fairly successful. The work done during the quarter just ended bore increasing testimony to the energy and usefulness of the Conven- tion, nevertheless he would still urge upon them the aecessity for further increased energy to combat every new device of the enemy. The maxim of each one ahould be "Work while it is day, the night cometh when no man can work." The C.S.J.T. (Bro. Vint. Ashton) reported excellent improvement in the juvenile branch of the order. The C.E.S. (Bro. Taylor Earlestown) re- ported considerable advance by the electors in various places returning candidates favourable to- the cause te the Town Councils. The Treasurer (Bro. Brockbank, St. , Helens) reported a very substantial balance in hand. The usual public meeting was then held, the Rev. T. .1. Bent presiding, supported by Bros. Morris Jones, D.C.T. ; Quartermaster-Sergeant J. W. Roberts, G. F. Clarke, Brockbank, Taylor, and others, and an excellent programme of songs, readings, and recitations .was gone through, the Baptist choir kindly assisting.
THE BICYCLE AS A REVOLUTIONIST.

, The " Arena " for October publishes an article upon the "Economical and Social Influence of the Bicycle," by Sylvester Baxter, which is supple- mented by the paper of Plfr. Flower upon the" In- fluences of the Bicycle tlpon Dress Reform." If the bicycle can reform women's dress, it is capable of refotmintanything in this world, and it would seem that it has actually begun its beneficent trans- formation.

• Mr. Flower says A few years ago the spectacle of a woman on a bicycle brought • lash of indignation to the face of the average matron ; to-day thousands of ladies in our great cities are enjoying this health-giving exercise, and even the universally loved and respected president of the Women's Christian Temperance Union chose a safety bicycle in preference to an outing at a resort distant from her charming home. The one drawback to women's ease and comfort on the wheel is the long skirt. The bicycle is one of the many agencies acting for reform.

Mr. Baxter, referring to ;the same subject in its wider bearings, says : The beneficent influence upon women might form the subject of an essay by itself. The bicycle has given, as nothing else has, the means for a healthful exercise combined with delightful recreation, so much needed by the six. It has gone far towards emancipating them from slavish conventionality in both dress and conduct. It has taught them the advantage of sensible and health- ful attire, an advantage which, once enjoyed, they are naturally reluctant to deprive themselves of in ordinary life. It has given them an independence in action ap- proaching that possessed by their brothers. In the parks of a great city, for instance, young ladies may daily be sees by the score, singly, or in groups, speeding freely everywhere upon their bicycles, with the same sense cf security, and appearing as much at home as they would be were they walking in the seclusion of their household gardens. It has also imparted a renewed strength to the natural associations between the two sexes, so health- fully characteristic of American life ; the informality of intercourse going far to break down the barriers which, , by. concealment and the consequent morbid curiosity that ,it.arouses, form a leading cause of immorality. Mr. Baxter gives a good deal of information as to Oho spread of bicycling in the United States. He mays ths.p there are twenty-seven different establish- ments deivOted to the manufacture of bicycles, and to supply these works s great number of other estab- lishments have been set up. The bicycle has ha 4 enormous influence in encouraging the construc- tion of good highways. The rage for railway con- struction has for years absorbed all the road-mak- ing attention of Americans; now they are begin- ing to devote their attention to the value of high roads. In calling attention to this subject the bicycle has been the chief constructor. Tnere are now twenty-five thousand Americans members of the League of American Wheelmen,and their united action has exercised a constant and beneficent,in- , &ewe upon the backward American world. Not fso, hat the bicycle has been the I,ea4ing faetor oniy in building uti tittri4Ctiv6 1614bUrba ane" " the leading cities. They 1e...41 °"'' establish t 4140 e es public parks, in which special bleyCl tracks al being laid out:— The writer recalls one important Western city where, on his first visit, the streets were in a wretched condi- tion, and there were, probably, not half a dozen wheel' men in the place. On a subsequent visit he found the streets beautifully paved with asphalt, and bicycles gliding swiftly around by the hundred, far outnumber- ing any ,ither forms of vehicles. Waxing eloquent on this theme, Mr. Baxter pre- dicts that the bicycle contains in itself the element of a new type of vehicle, which will Come into universal 116e', with the supplanting of animal trac- tion by electricity. Horses will disappear from the roads as they have disappeared from most of the tramways. Perfectly smooth pavements will follow, constructed upon the most scientific principles, and as they will no longer be pounded to pieces by horses' hoofs, their cost of maintenance will be minimised. Multitudes of light vehicles of various sizes impelled by electricity will speed noiselessly in every direction. All the noise and rattle of the steeet practically will vanish, and with it much of the nervousness of the city dwellers. Street clean- ing will become almost a sinecure. The effect of bicycling on holiday-making has hitherto been but imperfectly appreciated. Here is a hint for Dr. Lunn :

For several years past a prominent bicycling clergy- man has been very successful in organising a series of vacation tours for his brethren of the cloth through various interesting portions of our own country. Altogether, Mr. Baxter's paper almost leads up to the conclusion that the simple combination of the indiarubber tire and the foot pedal is likely to pro- ' duce- 'Moire far-reaching effects upon the social, moral, intellectual,end physical life of the world than a New Religion.

win—it win not lessen what I have uone—it will not restore your love to you. If / cannot have your love, I know this—that lonic: Lawrence, my rival, never can,"

Arthur Rochester stretched out his hands with a terrible cry, "My Clod 1 my God, Elaine I I cannot believe this You could not be so inhuman as to see that poor girl drown before your eyes and not call for help," be groaned in anguish. "I would do the same thing over again!" cried Elaine, "I glory in the thought, that if your love is not for ine, my rival is beyond the reach of it. Always remember that, Arthur Rochester I"
CHAPTER XXXI. "YOU MUST FORGET HER; HER LOVE IS NOT OR YOU."
It was the most intensely thrilling moment of Arthur Rochester's life. He stood like a man turned to stone, as he listened to the fatal truth as to lonie's fate, as it fell from her rival's _ _

-"Elaine," he cried, hoarsely, "if I were to believe you for one moment, I should go mad." "All I have told you is quite true," she replied. "The f;irl is dead. She will never come between your love and me again." With a bitter groan, wrung from the very depths of his tortured heart, Arthur turned and strode away, No mortal man was ever in a more cruel situa- tion.

Should he give to the world Elaine's confession, thus unravelling the terrible mystery surrounding lonie's disappearance? Or, seeing it could not bring life back to his dead love, let matters rest where they were? The long interval that had Intervened would preclude all possibility of finding the body. Only Heaven knew the pangs it cost him to decide so hard a question. How he cried out to the listen- ing angels to forgive Elaine if they could, for he never should. She had not plunged a dagger into the girl's white breast. She had not held a draught of poison to her lips. Still it was murder, to stand there and see her rival perish before her eyes, and not ory out for help when it was so near at hand, to save her.
That evening he wrote a short note to Elaine, which ran as follows:

"MISS GRANGER—MADAM: I leave my father's house to-night—aye, within this hour. The roof which shelters you can never shelter me. Meeting you would be simply torture for me. I could not look upon your hands without feeling that there were crimson stains upon them which nothing could wash away. May Heaven pardon you for what you have done, for I never shall.

"ARTHUR." , Mr. Rochester heard of his son's intended de- -1 pasture with the greatest consternation, as did his sister. "He has quarrelled with Elaine," he said, help- lessly. "She will give me no satisfaction about the matter, but goes about pale as death. He refuses to speak on the subject. There never was r young man who has so much trouble with his love affairs, it appears to me." "It has all come abovt by your interfering in these love affairs, in the first place, John," returned I Hilda Rochester, quietly. Everything has gone LI all wrong with Arthur ever sinct: ." It with! one wish of My life to see him hop thar p.ot married to Riau.— I fall ,res_i through," retorted the llionaire, "Every effort must be made to re-CMaclie the lovers." When Arthur was broached tipeNhe subject a little later, he grew white as death. "For heaven's sake, never refer to this again, father," he cried, "or you will drive me mad. Try to believe that all is over between Elaine an, myself. She shall never be wito pi mine. Neyer I" "It can only be some foolish love& quarrel," declared Mr. Rochester. "You must not let that wreck the happiness of a life-tlsne." I know best, father," returned Arthur. "The very sound of her name is most distasteful to me. I am going where I shall never see her face again— never while I live." There was so much concentrated bitterness in his voice that whatever his father's doubts might have been before, they settled down into positive eonvic- tion now; that all was indeed over between his son and his beautiful ward. When Arthur took his departure, a face white as marble watched him from the lace-draped windows of an upper room. "He has gone out of my life for ever," muttered Elaine. "I have lost him; but even in this hoar of torture I am exultant at the thought that my rival cannot win him. He has kept my secret—not out of respect for' me—but to spare her memory. I should never have told him the fatal truth, but that he goaded me to frenzy, and in an unguarded moment it fell from my lips. Ah me—au me I why should love be called the world's blessing, I wonder, while to so many women it proves so bitter a curse. I, too, shall leave this place. I cannot stay where every room is haunted by his face," she muttered. All in vain Mr. Rochester tried to persuade her to remain, when Elaine made known to him her decision the next (lily. "But, my deer, where would you go?" he ex- claimed in bewilderment. "This has been your heme since you were a little child. A young gist cannot go out into the world alone. Besides, I Imagine that when Arthur'a anger has had time to cool, he will return to you. The course of true love never did run smooth,' you know." "He will never be any more to me than he is now," she answered, slowly, as she turned abruptly away. The next afternoon Elaine left her guardian's 'house, taking Patrice, her maid, with her. No one felt regret, save old Mr. Rochester, for the wilful, petted heiress had not been much of a favourite among the servants of the household. Their destination was a small village in the in- terior of the State. "I want to get away from the sight and the sound of the water, Patrice,' she said, as the train steamed out of the depot. "I can always fancy I hear the wash of the waves against the aide of a boat; and the sound fills me with terror." Leaving them for the present, we will return to that fatal night on which lonie Lawrence was left alone to the mercy of the white-capped waves, to live or die, as Heaven saw fit. A wild cry fell from lonie's lips as she dis- uovered herself falling, but the shrill whistle of the yacht, as she skimmed over the waters, drowned it. From the time she struck the water, Heaven was kind to her. Unconsciousness claimed her, and the awful horror of the situation was robbed of its mighty terror.

LUNATICS AT PARBSIDN. With reference to the maintenance of lunatics at Park side Asylum the Local Government Board wrote stating that they were not aware of any legal objections to the payment of the extra charges, assuming that an order of the justices had been obtained.
HR. BR-lINNER ON THB TAXATION OF COPYHOLD MANORS.

Letters had been received from the Local Government Board, Mr. Alan de Tatton Egerton, M.P., Mr. Henry Tellemache, MP., and Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., ack- nowledging the receiPt of the resolution of the Board in favour of the rating, for all parochial purposes, of the incomes of copyhold manors. Mr. Brunner added "I am entire in sympathy with the purpose of tha resolu- tion, and Mould have been still better pleased with it if the Guardians had included ground rents and the esti- mated annual value of unoccupied lands in towns. There are,Such plots of land within the Runcorn Union, which have, through the expenditure of public money in our own time enormously increased in value, whilst their eiviers have paid not one penny in rates, or for that matter in taxes only." The other gentlemen made no observations on the resolution. APPOLMTMHNT OF SCHOOLMISTRESS. There had been four applications received for the posi- tion of schoolmistress In the House, and Miss Eliza Brereton, of Sandbach, and Miss Elizabeth Moran, of Walsall, Staffordshire, appeared before the Board. Even- tually Miss Moran was appointed.

div.head: TUB LOCAL GOVERN/eI—ENT BOARD AND DISTRESS.
div.p: TUB LOCAL GOVERN/eI—ENT BOARD AND DISTRESS.

The circular issued by the Local Covernment -Board was submitted, stating that from information which the Board had received it appears that there is at the present time a considerable amount of distress in different parts of the country, occasioned by scarcity of employment, and it is probable that this condition of things may become more general and be more intensified in the course of the winter. The circular then sum- marizes the letter issued by the previous Board in the spring ot 1886, pointing out that any relaxation of the general rule respecting able-bodied male applicants requiring she acceptance of an order for the Workhouse or the performance of an adequate task of work would be most disastrous. What is needed is work which does not involve the stigma of pauperism, which all can perform, and which does not compete with that of other labourers, and it is not likely to interfere with the resumption of regular employment. The circular suggests spade husbandry on sewage farms, laying out of open spaces, cleansing of streets, and laying out new streets. It is suggested that the wages paid should be somewhat Ina than are usually paid for similar work. In suitable cases the local authcrities may be sure that that there will be every desire to deal promptly with applications for a loan. The President urges that works should be commenced at an early date.—Mr. Taylor said he was not aware that they had much, if any, dis- tress in the district.—Mr. Heywood said the Ship Canal had found employment for all who wpuld work. (Hear, hear.)
TOBACCO AND SNUFF.

A general order moved by the Local Government Board, was read, empowering the Guardians to allow tobacco or snuff to such Workhouse inmates, who are not able bodied, or who are employed upon work of a specially disagreeable character, as the Guardians ns ay consider should be supplied with the same.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
NARROW ESCAPE pF DRIVER AND FIREMAN.

The driver of an engine et Stobcross Dock, Glasgow, on Wednesday night, reversed the machinery to avoid a collision with a goods train, and he and the fireman jumped off. The engine bounded in the opposite direc- tion and dashed into a coal train, smashing several trucks. The engine overturned and the boiler burst. No- body was injured.
.. THE ALLEGED FORGERY BY A DOCTOR.

At the Old Bailey on Thursday, Dr. Francis Charles Scott Sanders pleaded guilty to forging bills of exchange amounting to £15,000 but Mr. Gill, on behalf of the prisoner, applied that the case might be adjourned until next sessions, as there were certain facts which he ' wished to place before the court in mitigation of punish- ment, the money not having been spent by prisoner upon himself, but in connection with the Lyric Club. The application was granted.

div.head: STARTLING DISCOVERY IN BRADFORD.
div.p: STARTLING DISCOVERY IN BRADFORD.

SUSPECTED OUTRAGE AND MURDER. On Thursday morning the body of a girl, four years old, daughter of a widow named Brown, living in Brooklyn-st., Bradford, was found partly buried in an ash heap near the Corporation refuse destructor, fianimersmith-st. The girl had been missing since Wednesday morning. There are marks of violence on the body, which led to the supposition that the child had been outraged and murdered,but a full medical examin- ation of the remains have not been made. Further par- ticulars seem to leave little room for doubt that the un- fortunate little girl had been outraged and murdered. Garner, tha rag picker, interviewed by our representa- tive, states that it was found lying on the side of a small heap of paper scraps and shop sweepings. The whole bpdy was covered with these scraps, and was laid bead downward and feet pointing towards the summit of the !yap.

div.head: DISAPPEARANCE OF THE TOWN CLERK OF RA WTENSTALL.
div.p: THE DISAPPEARANCE OF THE TOWN CLERK OF RA WTENSTALL.

THE ALLEGED DEFALCATIONS. Up to the present nothing has been heard of the miss- ing Town Clerk of Rawtenstall (Mr.. Walter Vera Station), against whom a warrant has been issued for embezzling £2OO. So far as the borough accounts are concerned, they appear to have been properly kept, and some of Station's friends clung to the hope that in the end all would be found right, even although he had written a letter confessing that he had misappropriated Corporation moneys. This hope was destroyed on Toes- day, when certain facts were brought to light which point to more than one serious offence having been com- mitted. Mr. Procter, of Burnley, be borough auditor. ! who is examining the accounts, Informed a cor- respondent that instances had been found in which persons had advanced considerable sums of money to Mr. Station on behalf of the Corporation, but which had never been handed over to the borough treasurer. One man living at Cloughfold has advanced £2OO, and the only receipt he possesses is the Town Clerk's acknowledgment of it, besides papers which prove that the Town Clerk paid the interest hinaself. Is another case a man named Natali advanced £2OO in April. 1889. and here the receipt bears the seal (if the old Local Board (Which was then in existence) and the forged signature of the gentleman who was chairman of the Board at that time. Mr. Station, it is stated, has for three or four years past acted as the trustee of an estate of about £3,000, which a young lady is entitled to when she attains her majority next month. Suspicion has been aroused that the funds of this estate may have been misapplied, and that the dread of discovery and the consequences that would follow induced Stallon to abscond. His plans appear to have been well laid, for quite a week elapsed before any serious alarm was felt at his disappearance and inquiry instituted concerning him. Of course in that time he may have got well clear of the country. 10' CONVENTION OF THE IRISH NATIONAL PARTY. A great Convention of the Irish National party was neld in Dublin on Tueld ay, at which a number of rev- , lutions were passed be aring on Home Rule, the Irish agricultural crisis, and the evicted tenants. A balance' sheet was submitted showing disbursements of £12,223 between February, 1891,and October 1892, and a balance in hand of £3O. Another statement giving the accounts of the general election fund showed disbursements or £17,120. Among the speakers was Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., who said that while the attitude of the Irish Parliamentary party towards the Liberals was perfectly frank and plain, and it was clearly understood that the Liberal party were riot only bound to give to Ireland a Parliament but also to put the question of Home Rule in the forefront until the measure was passed into law. That did not imply that the Irish members were to blind themselves to the difficulties of the situation, or to refuse to assist the Liberals in carrying English measures of reform. The agricultural crisis in Ireland he regarded as wor...s than the famine of 1879. It was their misfortune in Ireland to have a landlord class in hostility to the national aspirations of the people. They were making appeals to the good sense of the landlords Pllld to their sense of justice, but not with any considerable hope. 1 They should not confine themselves to appeals. He did not wish to threaten, but he wished to warn the Irish landlords that the spirit of Ireland was not broken, and ' that the day had gone by when Irish people would suffer themselves to perish in their own land. With reference to the Evicted Tenants Commission. he said the reason ; they felt confidence in the result of it was that in their judgment no honest or open mind could come to any other conclusion than that the cause of the tenants was just, moderate, and wise. Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P., Mr. Sexton, M.P., and Mr. Michael Davitt, M.P., also de- livered addresses, and the last named moved a resolu- tion in which the Irish members were asked to be in their places in Parliament not only when Irish questions were being discussed, but also when questions affecting the welfare of the working-ciwees of Great Britain were under consideration.

div.head: PRIDE OF THE MILL
div.p: PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BY LAIJEA JEAN LIBBEY

CHAPTER XXX. "IP I CANNOT HAVE YOUR LOVE, MY RIVAL NEVER SHALL." Elaine Granger decided then and there that she would never lose Arthur Rochester without a desperate struggle. If he left the decision with her, he should never go free. A love like hers must win its object, if it lay within human power. She would rather have been Arthur Rochester's wife, though he despised her—his wife, to lavish her unreciprocated love upon, live in the light of his presence—than to have wed a king on his throne who might worship her. There would be little help for him if the decision rested in the hands of her who was deaf to all other prayers save her deep desperate love for him. She stood before him with clasped bands, and the pain on her face was pitiful to behold. "Could you never learn to care for me, Arthur?" she cried. "Am I not as fair as she whom you love ? No other woman will ever love you as deeply and truly as I do I Oh, Arthur, pause and think what it is that you ask when you wish me to give you up l" He took her cold, little, trembling hands in his. He could not help feeling touched. So much love lavished upon him in vain I He felt inexpressibly sorry for Elaine—for her distress and her humilia- tion in telling him this. "You will never know bow I struggled against 'this love with my heart and soul, for I knew I stood pledged to you. But I find," he continued, sadly, "that a man cannot say to his heart, 'Thou shalt love this one, not that one,' for a power stronger than man's controls the heart, and we are powerless to resist loving to the end of life the one whom heaven Intended for us."

"That is what my heart pleads to you, oh, false one," sobbed Elaine. A distressed look broke over Arthur's handsome, honest face. "I have been more honourable than some men would have been in such a case," he answered. "Not no in a thousand would have come to you and stated the case, pleading with you for forbear- ance."

_ Ah. Arthur," she cried, "forget this other love, and be true to your pledge to me. Put her away from your thoughts. Thrust her from your heart'. "My dear Blaine," he answered, huskily, "if I could but persuade you that that is impossible. I am so grieved at being obliged to tell you all this that I cannot find words to express my sorrow. Be reasonable, Blaine." "Love like mine knows no reason," she answered. bitterly. "I ask you once more: Will you give her up?" "I can never love another," he answered, sadly. k would care for you if I could, Blaine, but, alas, cantint." • ' s tow "Will you never love me?" she asked, in a 7 breathless, intense tone that might have warned him of his coming danger. "I will not deceive you, Elaine, or build your , poor heart up on false hopes. I can never love you as I should the woman whom I would call my wife," "You have changed my whole life, Arthur," she cried, shrilly, "and there is such a thing as love turning to the bitterest hate in a single instant; and I hate you now even as passionately as I have ever loved you. I will torture your heart, pain for pain, as you have tortured mine." "Elaine! Elaine !" cried Arthur. "In Heaven's name, calm yourself! You distress me greatly l" He never forgot the look she turned upon him while his life lasted. Here was a side of the girl's nature he had never dreamed of, and he thought of the line— " Hell bath no fury like a woman scorned." "I will have a glorious revenge upon you!" she cried. "It is sweet to me to know that I have parted you from the one you love forever. I could have saved her for you, but no, I would not." Arthur looked at her in astonishment. He quite thought the sorrow which she had taken so deeply to heart had turned her brain. A terrible laugh fell from her lips that sent the blood through his veins in a cold chill. "Yes, I could h ve saved her," she muttered, "but I found out it was she whom you loved." He was convinced more than ever, by these incoherent words, that Elaine was losing her reason. "You think I am going mad, but you will shortly see a method in my madness that will shock you, I tinny." "Elaine," he said, "pray say no more." His soothing tone exasperated her. "Have you ever settled it in your mind what became of your love on the night of that yachting party ? " she asked, shrilly. "You see, lam not so mach of a dupe as you have imagined me to be. Hark—hear me through; do not interrupt me, and I will tell you and the world where to find your love." " E4aine, you most be mad—quite mad I " be answered, sadly. "You have strange hallueina- tioaa." "You will not persist in saying that much longer," she cried. And there was such profound emotion, such a look on her face, that, even against his own will, her words were carrying a strange thought to his shocked heart. There was such an irresistible ring of truth in her voice that no one could doubt that she knew what she was saying. He felt com- pelled to listen. " You remember that night of the yachting party,' she continued, "while I shall never forget It. It was in the grounds of the villa where we stopped for luncheon that I first found out my lover's perfidy. Muhl" she cried again, as he was about to speak. "Hear me through. div.head: THAT CLOCK IN OXFORD-STREET.
div.p: THAT CLOCK IN OXFORD-STREET.

You may see it from the top of a 'bus any day. It is on the outside wall of a building a short way west of the Circus. Sometimes this clock is right, sometimes wrong : and erewhiles it takes a rest and never moves a hand. Then it feels refreshed and goes ahead again. On the dial is this inscription : " Delay not ; time flies." Let us hope that the 'bus drivers and messenger boy*. will lay the impressive fact to heart. For time flew be- fore clocks were invented,and it flies just the same when wheels break and weights go to sleep at the bottom of the clock cases. Whether we dream or wake, laugh or. cry, make money or lose it, Time keeps his wings flap— ping. The morning cometh and also the night, no 'nat— ter whether weddings or funerals are sandwiched be— tween them.

Now suppose we apply the principle, and first name a, date—the year 1889. In November of that year a cer- tain gardener, in pursuit of his vocation, csught what.. he calls (like the rest of us) a " chill." This " was not the result necessarily of exposure to cold, for people "catch colds" and have " chills " in the hottest weather. This is queer, considering the names we give' to these sensations. In very truth we are overtaken with them oftener in summer than in winter. Why so F' Because in the proper sense they are not chills at all, but a nervous disorder arising from low vitality and some kind of poison in the blood. Most fevers begin with a. chill, although the thermometer may show 100 degrees. of heat. So much for that. It is worth storing away in your memory.

After the chill the gardener found that something ailed his ankle ; he could walk only with difficulty. A fortnight later he could not walk at all. When he moved his foot the pain made him feel faint. This was bad, especially for a man whose work positively re- quired him to use his I.egs. He sent for the doctor, who ordered him to bcci and wrapped up his legs in cotton wool. Then, it goes without saying, he began swallow- ing doses of medicine. A week more and he woo. covered all over with large boils. He was now in con— dition to understand one at 19ast of the afflictions of Job.

As to the boils they were the result of nature's effort to expel the poison from this man's blood. Nature does nothing from mere whim, neither does she love to tor- ment any of her children. But people don't perceive this, and so they try to dry the boils up, or drive them in, while she tries to make them little volcanoes to carry off the inside fire. Oblige the writer by remembering this also.

Fnom Una coint on we will let the gardener tell his own tale. He says f :was in a sad plight. I had my club doctor attending me for thrtxl weeks, but got worse and feared I was going to be laid up f..,"r a long time: The pain seemed fixed in my knees, and I suffeteti intensely. I had another month of this and then golt relief in a way I will tell you of. While I was OM ITIT back and my work waiting for me, a book—a small paper-covered one—was left at my house. It told of Mother Seigel's Syrup, and how a case like mine was cured by that medicine. I sent at once to Mr. Smith's, stores, at Penge, and got a bottle, and found relief almost directly ; for Igot the medicine on the MondaYr and by the following Friday I was able to walk two miles. On the next Monday I went to my work, and have never had any return of the ailment since. I think the chill put my blood out of order.—A. GEORGE, 15,South1 str., Penge, near London.

In his last conjecture Mr. George is mistaken. It WAS. not the chill that put his blood out of order, but it was his blood being out of order that gave him the chill, arid also the boils and the attack of acute rheumatism that trailed after. How long do you suppose it is going t*" ' take us to teach the people of England that rheuinat.isva is an inflammation of the joints and muscles caused by uric acid in the blood, and that this acid arises from ler- mented food in the stomach—indigestion and dyspepsia ? We can't say ; but we shall keep on lecturing them till they do learn it. Then when they groan and howl from gout, rheumatic, and other sorts of explosions of inncr stomach poisons, they will shorten their Fufferi no by taking Seigel's Syrup to drive out the poison. Say this to your- self over and over : "Almost all the pangs and ills ever suffered from, or ever will, are symptoms of indi- gestion and dyspepsia," and you'll finally possesS the biggest nugget of wisdom you ever had in your life. As to that clock in Oxford-street, if Mr. George Nob timed himself by it when he was ill, he would, on get- ting out again, have found himself six weeks late. For time flies, even when a man can't employ an hour of ate advantage.

The circular suggests sped husbandry on sewage fartriSt laying out of open spaces, cleansing of streets, and Jay-- log out new streets. div.head: FRONT WARRINGTON TO
div.p: FRONT WARRINGTON TO
RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT
COMMISSIONERS.
PURCHASE OF WATERWORKS.

On Tuesoay evening a meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners was held at the Town Hall for the purposi of considering a, proposal of the Finance Cammittee, to purchase the Runcorn, Wes- ton, and Halton Waterworks. Mr. F. Wiswall, the chairman, presided, and these were present : Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., W. Fisher, J. Pritchard, J. Meadowcroft, J. W. Lightburit, H. Coward, R. Abel, P. Smith, D. Bisbrown, W. Leach, T. Lea, R. W. Humphreys, W. Hankin4on, F. A. Lake (law clerk) and E. Marshall (secretary.) On the motion of Mr. Fisher, seconded by Mr. Speak- man, the Board resolved into Committee. After the lapse of an hour and twenty minutes, the representatives of the press were called into the room, and the follow- ing letter addressed to Mr. Lake, from Mr. Ashton, solicitor to the Waterworks Company, was read. " Runcorn, 15th November, 1892. Dear Sir,—Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company. Referring to my letter of the 11th inst., I have to inform you that the directors, at their meeting yesterday, resolved that the report of their Committee be received and adopted, that is to accept the offer made to purchase the Water- works undertaking, namely, (1) a cash payment of £87,500 ; (2) the stock, coals, meters and stores to be taken at a valuation ; (3) the Company to take the revenue and pay all outgoings up to the date of the transfer : (4) the Commissioners to insert in their Act all necessary clausee for winding up the Company, a pro- visional agreement to be entered into, embodying the terms, without prejudice however, until such agree- ment is completed, and they will call a meeting of their shareholders as soon as practicable for the purpose of obtaining their sanction thereto." . The Law Cletk then produced the following report of the Finance sub-Committee :—On the sth May last yesr you appointed a sub-Committee to consider the advisa- bility of purchasing for the town the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks. We, therefore, beg to report that on the 19th May, your Committee opened neweie- tiens through the Law Clerk with the directors of the Waterworks Company, and statements of their accounts for the past ten years were kindly furnished, and the same were very carefully considered by your Committee. We append a statement of the accounts, as furnished by the Company's solicitor, to the Law Clerk, for the year ended 30th June last, and your Committee would observe that the Company have based their negotiations for sale upon the figures therein stated : Revenue for year ended 30th June, 1892, £4,585 19s. 7d. Expenditure Ordinary.

£ e. d. Interest on Debenture and Pre- Serena:. Stock 939 17 0 Salaries and Wages Coals Rent and Way-leave Oil, ke. 73 10 10 Stationery. !se. 261 16 10 Rates and Taira Servioe Pipes 246 5 4 Sundries £2785 19 7

Net Income last year available for • litivldend The terms were as follows : Ordinary Shares 25 yeare purchase on present £ 8. d. net income of Company (£:800) Preference 3hares-30 years' purchase of inte- rest payable 24182 0 0 Debentures Depreciation Fund Value of Unused Stock 450 0 0 Office Furniture, 8c 6O 0 0 Parliamenttry Expenses, b.c 1530 0 0

Also such sum of money as should represent the amount of revenue and profits of the company at the date of the transfer. Your committee did not see their way to entertain this offer of the company, and they made counter pro- posals. Protracted negotiations ensued, and eventually the following terms were agreed unon, subject to the approval of this Board and the shareholders of the Waterworks Company. A cash payment of £67,500 made up as follows : £ s. d. Ordinary Shares -25 years' purchase of a yearly net income of 11,575 Preference Shares-28 years' purchase of inter- est Winding up lizpenses—Compeneation to der- 'rants. au Debentures

The Stock, Coals, Meters, and Stores to be taken at a valuation. The Company to take the Revenue and pay all out- goings up to the date of transfer. The Commissioners to insert in their Act all necessary clauses for winding up the Company. Your Committee believe the terms named are very favoutable for the ratepayers, and they have been unable to learn of any other Public Authority purchas- ing works of the like kind by so satisfactory an arrange- ment. In the event of the Commissioners becoming possessed of the Waterworks, your Committee estimated the finan- cial results will be as follows : i. d. 2 s. d.
Net Revenue from water supply, Ac , per annum Interest on Oapital of say £71,900 at 31 per cent. Annual Payment to Sinking Fund fore period of 55 years 5lB 0 0 2826 0 0

if the capital be repaid on the annuity principle, 55 years at 3-1 per cent.--Annual amount required £2,787. In several cases Parliament has sanctioned the sus- pension of payments to the Sinking Fund for the first five years. This would leave a balance in favour of the Board for the aforesaid period if £207 a year. The ratepayers will thus have little, if any deficit to make up, whilst in a few years it is confidently anticipated that tkere will be a satisfactory surplus. Your Com- mittee recommended the Finance Committee to agree to the terms before named, and to take the necessary 'Lena for carrying the same into effect. In submitting this report your Committee are pleased to acknowledge the courtesy and the reasonable spirit displayed by the directors of the Waterworks Company, in the negotia- tions which have taken place. Signed Wm. Fisher, chairman, J. W. Lightburn, J. Meadowcroft, J. Pritch- ard, P. Speakman, P. Wiswall. At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held on the 11th inst., the foregoing report was approved and adopted, and the Finance Committee recommended it to the Board for approval and adoption. Mr. Fisher moved the following resolutions :—That the recommendation of the Finance Committee to pur- chase the undertaking of the Runcorn, Weston, and Balton Waterworks Company, on the terms mentioned in Mr. Ashton's letter of this date, be, and it is hereby adopted. That Mr. John Weston, CE. Manchester,be requested to inspect the well, engines, reservoirs and plant of the Waterworks Company, and report as to the condition thereof, and also as to the best means of connecting the I main of the Liverpool Vyrnwy aqueduct, at Norton, I with the existing system of pipes of the Company, both with a view to the immediate requirements, and the I future supply of the district. That Mr. J. L. Tunstall, of Warrington, be requested to examine the accounts of the Waterworks Company, and the terms of the proposed purchase thereof by the Commissioners and to report thereon, and as to the inancial prospects thereof. That the Law Clerk be and he is hereby instructed to prepare a Bill to enable this Authority to purchase the Waterworks for the improvement of the district and other purposes, and to take all necessary steps for the passing of such Bill into an Act, and that Mr. Chas. E. Balter.of 22,Great George-it., Westminster,be instructed as Parliamentary Agent. Hr. Lightburn seconded the motion. Mr. Speakman had great pleasure in supporting the motion. He felt sure from the price the Commissioners were paying for the works, that they would be of great advantage tithe present generation and of still greater benefit to future generations, who would honour the Commissioners of this day for buying the works. The community ought to know that they had an agreement with the Liverpool Corporation, which was incorporated in their Water Act, by which the Commissioners could have water from the Vynwry Aqueduct at a minimum and maximum price for given quantities. Mr. Ilurephreys also supported the resolution. They might congratulate themselves that they had an oppor- tunity of acquiring the Waterworks at a distant date, and he hoped it would not be a long time before they would als-i have control of their own lighting as well. Mr. Pritchard said he had every confidence in recom- mending these minutes for the approval of the Board. He thought the works would probably turn out to be, if not immediately, eventually of great advantage to the ratepayers at large. He strongly held the opinion that the Waterworks ought to be in the possession of the public authority, and under their control, he thought that opinion was largely held at the present time by the large shareholders of the Waterworks Company, and on that account he thought they had manifested a very reasonable disposition in entertaining the terms whereby they could arrive at a basis on which the transfer of the works could be brought about. There were two or three distinct advantages to be obtained. The Commissioners would be enabled by a small expendi- ture of capital, to connect with the Vyrnwy scheme,and be able to get an unlimited supply of water on very favourable terms. By that means water of an exceed- ingly good quality would be within reach of the rate- payers. In addition to this those ratepayers who had gone through the accounts, had observed that there was an increasing revenue year by year, and they hoped this transfer would be no burden upon the ratepayers, aud eventually he believed they would prove to be a source of financial advantage, and that a surplus would be derived from it. The agreement might be considered a fair one, and under present circumstances he thought the directors as well as the Commissioners, saw each their privilege in this agreement.—Neither one nor the

Mr. Risbrown in supporting the motion, said he did not think there was a gentleman present tut agreed that the Waterworks should be under the control of the local authority ; it would be sheer nonsense to argue to the contrary ; and they had there a going concern, and as far as they could judge from information obtained, in fairly good condition, and he thought they were taking a step in the right direction if they could get Parliamen- tary sanction. The following figures taken from the balance sheet for the half-year ended June last will be of interest :—The I debtor side of the capital account contains the following items :—Three thousand shares at £lO each, £30,000; preference stock, £20,000; depreciation fund, £1,000; debenture stock, £2,400. On the credit side there is a gross expenditure to December 31, 1891, of £53,233 Is. 4d., and the sum of £2 18s. is put down for exten- sion of mains in Egerton-at. There is therefore a balance of £lB4 Os. Bd. to form a reserve fund. In the general statement the assets are put down at £1.741 10s. 5d., made up as follows :—Cash in hand, £27 75.; amount owing for water by meter, fittings and water rent, £1,240 Bs. ed. ; stock of goods in worlshop and meters on hire, £284 4s. 10d. ; stock of goods at the pump- ing stations, £BO 10s. id.; extra buckets, valves, pipes, and fittings, £7B; coals, £33. The liabilities amount to exactly the same total, made up of balance due to capital account, £164 Os. Bd. ; balance due to revenue account, £997 41. 11d. ; owing for coals and to tradesmen, £l6 ss. 3d. ; owing to Parr's Banking Com- pany, £431 Bs. 4d. ; suspense accounts, being dividends ordered to be retained, £9B 2s. ed. ; cheques running, £39 2s. 9d. The balance sheet shows a profit on the half-vear's working of £997 4s. lid., including £242 7s 3d., brought from previous half-year, and, after paying a dividend of 5 per cent., there was a balance carried forward to the current half-year of £247 4s. 11d. At the date of the balance sheet, August Bth, it was reported that" the machinery and plant are all in good working order." For a considerable number of years after the company was formed no dividends were paid, and shares changed hands at so low a figure as £5, hut for the last ten years dividends have been paid varying from 3 per cent. to 5 per cent.

div.head: JOLLY PLACE AT ELECIION TIMES.
div.p: A JOLLY PLACE AT ELECIION TIMES.

At the hearing of the petition against the return of Hr. Frank James, Conservative member for Walsall, on Wednesday, a considerable body of evidence was given in support of the allegation of "general treating." If the witnesses are speaking the truth, Walsall must have been a merry place for the party of beer at election time. Enthusiastic publicSne provided lakes of beer " for which nobody paid or was asked to pay," and there were promises of further supplies if the candidate whom the "trade "supported was returned. Witnesses deposed that, In addition to the "free "drinks, quanti- ties of beer ware openly paid for by "prominent "Con- servatives. One ardent politician was reported to have delivered this brief but stirring speech : You vote for James and get him in, and we'll have the biggest barrel of ale that lean lift up to the table." Patriotic voters went about the borough shouting " James for aver" and obtaining free drinks at various public. houses.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouen on Tuesday. Mr. J. Mclntyre presidki, aritl there were-present the-Rev. J.- W.- N. Tanner, 'Messrs. J. Knowles, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, J. M. Wil- liam% J. t•raith, J. Whitlow, J. Parr, W. Whitlow, H. E. Heywood, J. Prandreth, W. Pickering, J. Weir; J. A 4hton (clerk); 6. Ashton (deputy clerk); J. Farrington (nuisance inspector). THE PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDGE.

Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. Runcorn, sth Nev., 1892. Dear Sir. Mersey Bridge. As promised I now enclose you copy of the resolution herein adopted by my Board at their last meeting. I may point out that such resolution was passed on the assumption that your authority either as a whole, or at least a part, would contribute to securing the £30,000. —Yours truly, Fred A. Lake. The resolution enclosed which has pre- viously appeared in the "Examiner," states that the Runcorn Commissioners resolve that it is desirable in the interests of the district of Runcern and the sur- rounding neignbourliood that the most efficacious steps should be taken to procure the construction of a bridge for vehicular and other traffic over the river Mersey between Widnes and Runcorn, at the earliest opportunity ind also that subject to the fulfillment of the following conditions, viz : (a) Author- ity to levy tolls for the use of the bridge for such a :period as may be necessary for the purpose next herein- latter mentioned. (b) The constitution of such tolls as la just charge to secure re-payment of the contributions ' hereinafter mentioned. (c) The creation of such rating areas as may hereafter be decided upon, and agreed to, and (d) the contribution of a like amount as that next hereinafter mentioned by the Widnes Local Board, or their successors. And (in order to meet the views of the committee of the Lancashire County Council) the Local Authority of Runcorn on the requisite Parliament- mentary sanction being obtained contribute a sum of £30,000 towards the cost of such undertaking, on the understanding that the balance of such cost is provided by the County Councils of Lancashire and Chew:1111(11. Hr. Heywood pointed out that the rateable value of Widnes was nearly three times as large as that of Run- corn, and as the district outside the latter town would benefit by the bridge, it was thought that it should can- tribute to Runcorn's share. But the subject was too large for a committee of five or ex to deal with,and he moved that the Committee be strengthened. It was thereupon resolved that the committee consist of Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Brandreth, John Baguley, W. Whit- low, II E. Heywood, J. Knowles, J. Parr, and John Whitlow.

THE PROPOSED INFECTIOUS. DISEASES MOSPITAL. The Clerk read the report of the committee, showing that Dr. Adams had submitted a sketch of what he con- sidered would suit the general requirements, and the Clerk laid before the committee tracings kindly lent by the Urban Sanitary Authority at Runcorn, of the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital built by them. Ile had made inquiries as to the cost of the hospital and caretaker's house, and had been informed that it had amounted to about £l,OOO. The committee were of opinion that a hospital and caretaker's house, built en the lines sug- gested by Dr. Adams, whieh were almost identical with that at Runcorn, would not exceed £1,200, and ought to be provided ; but inasmuch as the Sanitary Authority could not deal with cases of infectious disease except when, in the certificate •f a legally qualified practi- tioner, it was shown that there was not proper lodging or accommodation for the patient, or that the patient was lodged in a room occupied by more than one family, an infectious diseases hospital would mainly be required for pauper cases, and as in such casts the whole of the Union would have to contribute to the expense of pro- viding the hospital, the committee recommended that the question of providing such hospital should not be considered by the Sanitary Authority alone,.but should be submitted to the full Board. Ile pointed out that if it were provided at the expense of the whole Union it might be built on the vacant land adjoining the Work- house, which seemed to be the most suitable situation for it, inasmuch as it was not only central, but there was a good supply of water. Moreover, the cost spread over the whole Union, assuming that the outlay would not exceed £1,200. and that the money could be bor- rowed from the Public Works Loan Commissioners for a term of 30 years, would not necessitate a rate of more than 1-13th of a penny in the £. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. ' Knowles, the report was adopted. It was afterwards submitted to the Board of Guardians. Mr. Taylor pointed out that the ratepayers of Run- corn were already paying for one hospital, and if that report were carried out they would be paying for two. Perhaps Runcorn Board of Commissioners would oppose such a proposition.—Several members pointed out that at present £2 a week bad to be paid for pauper patients in the Runaorn hospital, and If a hospital were built at Dutton this would be no longer done. Runcorn,.it was pointed out, by reason of its large population, had most pauper cases, and ought to contribute its share to the hospital. Eventually it was decided that the Runcorn Guardians (Messrs. Taylor, Lea Norman, Speakman and Dr. Gastaldi), should be added to the Committee of the Rural Sanitory Authority in order that the sub- ject might be thoroughly thrashed out. OUTBREAK OF SMALLPDX ON THE SHIP CANAL. GRAVE SITUATION.

The Medical Officer reported as follows have to report that smallpox has broken out at the Ship Canal Huts, Moss Side, Moore. One patient, • navvy, voluntarily delivered himself up to the Warring- ton Smallpox Hospital, on the Bth inst. The other two patieata are children. On receipt of the information concerning the disease, I visited the huts and forthwith re-vaccinated every person in the hut where the disease , had broken out. 38 hours afterwards I re-vaccinated ' every man,wornan,and child in the entire colony of huts, save 6 men who had refused and gone to work. The huts at Bobs Bridge, Moore, and at Acton Grange, will all be re-vaccinated within 38 hours. It is impossible to say how far the epidimio will extend into your district, but I feel it incumbent upon me to point oat to you that you are utterly unprepared to deal with any extension, and that the only chance you have ever had of dealing with your cases)! infectious disease, namely. removal to Vrarnngton Hospital is denied to you, because the facili- ties of Warrington are now exhausted, and will be for at ' least six months. Nothing remains but re-vaccination, but you have no compulsory powers of forcing this. The district should be placarded forthwith calling upon every one to seek the protective effects of vaccination and re-vaecination ; disinfection of the ordinary kind by fumigation, dm„ is useless. It is impossible to estimate the gravity of the situation. The only consolation lies in the fact that bv my prompt information to the Ship Canal authorities and their acquiescence in any direc- tions there will be no one under their control not re-vac- cinate:l within 48 hours, within the immediate circle of infection. Great credit is due to them in this regard, and it affords me much gratification in being able to record it.—ln reply to the Chairman, the Medical Officer said he did not know what the Authority would do if the disease extended,as it perhaps would. He had found that six or seven grown up children at the Ship Canal huts had not been vaccinated at all. Mr. Brandreth said he supposed the patients at Moos Side were fairly well isolated.—Dr. Adams replied that they were so well isolated that men were going daily from the huts where the disease exists, into the bottom of the canal

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday afternoon at the Town Hall. There were present, Messrs. R. Heaton (chai:man), W. Balharry, (senior vice-chairman), W. Houghton. (junior vice-chairman), E. Au-Mend, J. Houghton, W. J. Shaw, G. Pilling, J. Hill, T. Smith, S. Davies, A. J. Jolley, J. Clarke, J. Dignum, J. Turton, G. Ratcliffe, A. Jolley, H. .1. Longton, the Rev. G. F. Robeits, and Messrs. J. C. Sutton, (clerk), S. Sutton, (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward, (master), and B. Shearer, (enquiry officer). HOUSI COMM MIR. This Committee reported an order that hereafter all in- mates over the age of 80, in the habit of using tobacco or snuff, and other inmates employed upon dis•greeable wok must be allowed one ounce of tobacco or half an ounce of snuff each, at the discretion of tha Master. The Committee also recommended that the usual Christ- mas dinner be provided for the officers and inmates.—The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Itercurvn.

div.head: SCHOOLS COSIXITTBE.
div.p: SCHOOLS COSIXITTBE.

A report of a meeting of this Commitee, specially con- vened to consider a letter by Mr. Jenner Fust was read. As to his suggestion for the provision of a playing field for the children, the ;Committee considered that the present means of recreation were most ample. As to fire arrangements they had appointed a sub-Committee consisting of Meesrs. W. Boughton, R. Heaton, Hill, Shaw, aukland, aid Ratcliffe to consider and report upon Mr. Jenner Fust's suggestion. The Committee concurred in Mr. Fust's suggestion that the boys be taught to knit. The Committee also announced that in order to carry out Mr. Fust's suggestion for the addition of books to the children's library, they would be pleased to receive contributions of books and magazines for the library.—The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. W. Hononrow. seconded by Mr. AnzLAND.
711 X BY•LiPDX EPIDIMIC.

1 The CLIRa said that since the last meeting of the Board, Dr. Thompson, Medical Inspector to the Local Government Board, had been over; and the Clerk read the following recommendations made by him :—The I abatement of the present epidemic of smallpox in War- rington, he pointed out, would principally depend upon the completeness and rapidity with which the influence of vaccination and re-vaccination could be applied. Everything which could possibly conduce to this end I should, therefore, be accomplished without delay. He approved of the vaccination officer's house-to-house visitation of the parts of the town most affected, about a I quarter of the borough, as promotive of this end. The remaining three-quarters should be similarly dealt with 1 with the utmost passible despatch, and for this purpose I he urged upon the Guardians the importance of ap- I pointing additional vaccination officers to aseist the pre- sent vaccination officer. And to give additional facilities to those at work daring the day, the public vaccination officer should attend at his station on one evening in I each week and preferably on the evening iof the day on I which he vaccinated infants in the morning, so that he iniglat have ample opportunity of providing himself with a sufficient supply of fresh lymph for the re-vaccination ;of the evening. It appeared to him that the proposal made by the public vaccinator that his vaccination station should for a time be opened two evenings a week instead of one for general vaccination was a wise and reasonable one, and he should therefore ask the Guar- dians to re-consider their decision adverse to this proposal. I The Clerk said he had seen the vaccination officer that I morning, and he told him that on the previous day the I number of people vaccinated by him was far in excess of the usual number.—The Chairman thought the Board ought to act on the advice of the Inspector.—Mr. I W. Houghton expressed his disappointment at the Board I not acceding to Dr. Gornall's application for extra vaccination facilities, and moved that the recommenda- tion of Dr. Thompson be acted upon and that Dr. Gornall be allowed another day a week for vaccination. —Mr. Longton seconded. Ile said that if Dr. Gornall had stated reasons for his request, it would have been unhesitatingly acceeded to. He thought it I was important that an additional vaccination officer 'should be appointed, and that the vaccination officer ought not to act as the medical officer in small-pox cases. (Cries of "Bear, hear.") It was not desirable that the I vaccination officer should be the means of propagating the disease by coming from amongst the patients to vaccin- ate people.—The Clerk said he was informed that Dr. Gornall', son exclusively attended to the cases in the hospital.—Mr. Clarke said he was sorry that nothing ' was recommended to the Board but vaccination.— Mr. Ratcliffe said he had heard that Dr. Gornall had I written to the Local Government Board, contrary to the decision of the Guardians.—Mr. Shaw : I believe that is so.—Mr. Ratcliffe said the doctor ought to have stated , his case to the Guardians before writing on his own account to censure them.—The Clerk, in answer to Mr. I Ratcliffe, said that was the rule of the Local Govern- ment Board to send him a copy of any letter sent them from the Union, but no copy of one from Dr. Gornall had reached him.—The Chairman said for that reason he told Mr. Ratcliffe that Dr. Gornall had not seat such a letter—Mr. Davies said it appeared in the newsoapers that a letter had been sent to the Local Government , Board.—Mr. Clarke expressed his opinion that every- thing else was being left undone except re-vaccination. He was sorry to find in the papers that Dr. (lonian spoke about 22 deaths, some of them through imperfect vaccination and said he could not say that any one ot the persons had been properly vaccinated. That was • very bad state of things. In answer to Mr. Ratcliffe, the Chairman said those who had died, and were reported as imperfectly vaccinated were vaccinated 24 to 30 years ago, and how were you going Ito find out how the original vaccisation was dons ? He osenfeesed he did not believe there was much truth in this matter of not being properly vaccinated.—A Guar- dian : Neither do I.—Mr. Longton : How is the medical officer to say whether they have been properly vaccin- ated if he did not attend—Mr. Clarke: It seems a muddle altogether. That is my opinion about it. After some futther discussion, the proposition was put and carried.—TheClerk said Dr. Watkins reported two cams of smallpox in the township of Ilaydock, but that the extension of the disease had been arrested by vaccination The doctor desired that the period for gratuitous vaccin- ation be extended ; and this was assented to by the Board.
THE UNEMPLOYED.
The circular letter to Boards of Guardians, from the Local Government Board with regard to the unemployed was read, but there was no discussion.

div.head: .ISLE OF MAN MURDER.
div.p: THE .ISLE OF MAN MURDER.
TRIAL OF COOPER.

At Douglas, fin Monday, George Barker Jai:nee Cooper. Manchester, was put on his trial before the Court ef General Goal Delivery for the murder of his wife at the Regent Hotel in Douglas. The Lieutenant Governor of the island (Mr. Spencer Walpole) presided, and the other members of the Court were the two Deemsters and the Clerk of the Rolls. The defence exercised the right of challenging the jury very fully, and the jurors who were finally sworn were mainly from the country dis- tricts. Mr. Cruickshank. in the absence of the Attorney General, opened the case for the prosecution. He de- scribed in detail the brutal conduct of the prisoner towards his wife and the threats he used on their arrival in Douglas the night before the murder. Com- ing to the consideration of the actual circumstances of the crime, he reminded the jury of the excuses the pri- soner had made when the body of the unhappy woman I was found on the bedroom floor, and contrasted them with the plea he had put in after having heard the ease for the Crown at the Court of Criminal Inquiry. A number of witnesses were examined, amongst them a photographer named Bradshaw, who, in cross-examina- tion by the prisoner's counsel, gave some remarkable evidence as to Mrs. Cooper's " vexatious " conduct towards the prisoner. The prisoner appeared to this witness to bea vary affectionate husband. The barmaid at the Regent Hotel proved that the prisoner having boasted of having given his wife a good thrashing—her eyes were blackened when she landed—and his threats as to " paying her out." At the adjournment for the day, the prisoner was detained in a cell under the court, in order to prevent the large crowd which had assembled Outside from making a hostile demonstration, as they were prepared to do, if he had been taken to the prison In Victoria-road.

The trial was returned on Tuesday. Evidence was given as to the finding of the body of the murdered woman in • bedroom at the Regent Hotel. The body was totally without covering when the prisoner admitted Mr. Weldon and other persons into the room. Questioned as to the circumstances of his wife's death, the prisoner replied that he had been to Dumbell's Bank and" found her like that "on his return. Attempts had been made to remove the traces of the crime, and it was clear from the condition in which the prisoner's clothing was found that he must have partially undressed himself after in- flicting the fatal wound. The stab caused death in less than ten minutes, brit the prisoner did not summon assistance, and a considerable time elapsed before he opened the door of the room. The police superintendent of Douglas related a conversation he had with the pri- soner,in which the latter suggested that he might escape with a few year's " transportation." The superinten- dent replied that the prisoner might be hanged, • remark which greatly agitated him. The surgeons who examined the body of Mrs. Cooper were called. Mr. O'Malley. the chief of these witnesses, gave some very remarkable evidence with regard to the wound in Mrs. Cooper's breast and the cut Us her night- dress. This mysterious cut, it seems, was not discovered until some time after the murder. Dr. O'Malley was cross-examined by the prisoner's advocate with the view of showing that the account which Cooper gave of the way in which the wound was inflicted might be correct. The defence, it will be remembered, is that Cooper sud- denly received a " stinging" blow from his wife, and that he "struck tack' in a moment, forgetting that he had a knife in his hand. The defence was never heard of until the case for the Crown was fully disclosed. Miss Louisa Cooper, sister of the deceased, gave evidence as to the cruelty of the prisoner to his wife when they were living in Higher Broughton, and afterwards at Old Trafford. The deceased's eyes were blackened, and on one occasion the prisoner bit her severely on the wrist. When the prisoner was not drunk he was a rule kind to his wife.

The trial was resumed at Douglas on Wednesday. Evidence was given by the brother of the murdered woman in proof of the cruelty with which she had been I treated. The witness on one occasion horsewhipped the 1 prisoner for his cruelty to his wife. The prisoner's ad- -1 vacate endeavoured to make the witness admit that 1 Mrs. Cooper herself supplied the whip, but the witness 1 maintained that it was given to him by one of the ser- vants. Mr. Superintendent /tent related the converse- bons he had had with the prisoner, and the warning he had given him in consequence of the reports of his cruelty; and a constable deposed to having hewed shrieks and screams proceed from the prisoner's bell- room. A considerable portion of the day was consumed in the endeavour by the prosecution to give secondary evidence with regard to a letter which the prisoner had written whilst in gaol. This part of the case involved reference to the divorce pr,ceedings which had been in- stituted against the prisoner by Mr. A. L Hunt. The 1 letter was sent to an address at New Brighton, and witnesses proved that the prisoner had lived there with Mrs. Hunt and" Harold Cooper," her little son. Wit- nesses were also called to prove that the prisener had been seen in Manchester with Mrs. Hunt. It is under- stood that Mrs. Hunt crossed to Douglas, with the prisoner and his wife, but since that night she has mysteriously disappeared, and the police have not been able to obtain the slightest clue to her where- aboute.

At the Cooper trial in Douglas on Thursday, the prose- cution put in a copy of the letter which the prisoner had written to Mrs. Hunt from gaol. It is a remarkable document. The prisoner says that he" loved the little girl "and had "raised. her from a barmaid to his own level." He" Peter imagined he would be placed in a suspicious light," and repeated that be " found her as stated in the papers and tried to bring her round :" the subsequent version being that he unwittingly struck her a fatal blow as she lay on the bed. After disposing of some property in Mrs. Hunt's favour, the prisoner expressed the intention to "travel for some years and blot out the memory of this business." After the letter had been. read two officers proved that at the police station the prisoner said to them it was "a sure case of suicide." The prosecution having closed their case, Mr. Ring poet- poiaed his speech to the jury, and called witnesses to show that the murdered woman was a person of bad character. The servants at No. 3,. West Clyne, were called, and they stated that Mrs. Cooper was of drenken habits. One of these witnesses, a girl named Bowles, said that Mrs. Cooper was "a quarrelling, nagging, drunken woman, and was drunk almost every day." Witness entered her service, however, without hesitation. She " thought she might do Mrs. Cooper a little good by going to her." Mr. Cell, the prosecuting counsel, suddenly produced letters which the witness had written to the relatives of the murdered woman. In these letters the witness expressed great sympathy with the family, and said that Mrs. Cooper's " trials and troubles" were over, and also spoke of her gentleness and patience. Mr. Gell asked the witness if the letters and her evidence referred to the same person,.and she replied that they did. The trial was again adjourned.

div.head: SCENE IN A POLICE COURT.
div.p: THE SCENE IN A POLICE COURT.

James Leaver, the gentleman and ex-Town Council-1 lor, who on Wednesday created a disgraceful scene in Blackburn Police Court, was brought up again on Thurs- day, charged with being drunk and disorderly in the 1 street and in the dock. He had been kept in the cells all night, and was evidently penitent. Be had nothing to say, except that he was very sorry. He was fined 158. and costs.

div.head: "FIERCE RACIAL CONFLICT."
div.p: A "FIERCE RACIAL CONFLICT."

The reporters at Homestead, Pennsylvania, describe a "fierce racial conflict" which occurred at Homestead between some negroes and the "strikers" from Mr. Car- negie's works. The fight was "desperate." and many revolvers were fired, but the most serious injury was done by a woman who was armed with a frying-pan. With this weapon she struck a negro on the head, and is reported—although the report is not com firmed—to have made some impression upon him.

div.head: NORTHAMPTON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE NORTHAMPTON TRAGEDY.
A CURIOUS INCIDENT.

The court was crowded at Northampton ABM Zel 1121 Thursday, when Andrew George Macrae, grocer's assis- tant, formerly wf Birmingham, was indicted before Mr, Justice Kennedy for the murder of Annie Pritchard, whose name has become familiar in connection with "the Althorp mystery." Mr. I3uszard, Q.C., who prose- cuted, was confident that he could trace the crime to the prisoner entirely by circumstantial evidence. On August 7th, the headless body of a woman tied in a sack bearing the name " E. Macrae, Northampton" was discovered in a ditch at Althorp, and in a warehouse owned by the prisoner's brother at Northampton were found some calcined bones believed to be part of the same body it would be proved that the prisoner synt amme time secretly in the warehouse, and that he was preturbed on quitting it ; and the proeemition maintained that he had murdered the woman and her child, and then en- deavoured to conceal or destroy the evidencse of his crime. At the adjournment for lnncheon a remarkable incident occurred. Ono of the jurymen" left the pre. , elects of the court" ta poet "an important letter," and the question arose whether in these circumstances the rtrial could proceed. His Lordship, after cousultation , with counsel, adjourned the case.

div.head: PETITION AGAINST MR. BALFOUR
div.p: THE PETITION AGAINST MR. BALFOUR

At the hearing of the East Manchester election peti- tion on Wednesday, at the Manchester A 5817.0 Courts, before Mr. Justice Cave and Mr. Justice Vaughan Williams, most of the day was taken up with the exam- ination and cross-examination of a hairdresser named , John Francis Green, until recently in business in the East Manchester Division- This witness declared that a Mr. Dodd told him he could put krirxt in the way of "making a trifle of money," and that as the result of their conferences bt was entrasted with two sums, £l5 and £7, which money he gave in varying amounts to persons who came to him, in accordance with a letter of instruction he received from Mr. Dodd. After the elec- tion Mr. Green heard that persons guilty a bribery were liable to imprisonment. Ile became alarmed, and after seeking advice he communicated with the petitioner, ; and then with the petitioner's soheitor. Some tickets and the letter off instruction which evidenced the trans- actions he had referred to were stolen, said the witness, from his house one evening in October, when he and his wife were teczporarily absent. The witness said he expected to receive £2OO AIN compensation for having had to give up his business tkrough giving evidence in this inquiry. Some additional evidence was adduced In , support of the charge of treating.

div.head: RESULT.
div.p: THE RESULT.

The hearing of the petition against the return of Mr. .I.J. Bailout, M.P., for least Manchester, was concluded on Thursday. Mr. Murphy, Q.C., called two witnesses with regard to the robbery at Mr. Green's bause, and then closed the case for the petitioner. Mr. Finlay, Q.C., at once submitted that no case bad been made out. Mr. Murphy /admitted that, as Mr. Green had said that Mr. Maltby was not the person he saw, there was no evidence of any communication between Mr. Green and an agent of the sitting member. He did not think in the circumstances thet he was justified in proceeding further. A number of witnesses, including Mr. Cheaters Thompson, were then put into the box by Mr. Finlay to contradict the statementa which had been made as to treating. The court. adjourned at this point,. and later in the day judgement was given. Mr. Justice Cave said that if the petitioner had been succeasfa it would have been necessary for the Court to consider in a great many cases whether they would not be compelled to order him to pay the costs of the charges with respect to which no evidence whatever had been given. He Mentioned this by way of caution that those who brought petitions should understand that they were not at liberty to throw charges about broadcast, but should confine themselves as far as reasonably could be done to those charges which they actually had the means or- expected to have the means of establishing. As to the story of Green, the barber, it was very- remarkable that no ono but himself had ever seen the. tickets of which he spoke. The negotiation by which- Green was to have £201) for his evidence—a negotiation. which did not reflect esedit on any party to it—mightt have had some influence on Green's mind. The whale story was so improbable that it was quite impos- sible to place any confidence whatever in it— indeed he was satisfied that the story was a fabrication, and that these tickets of Green's never had any existence except in his own brain. Be should like to remark that wheri4 man was so. much given to promiscuous treating as Mr. Tunstall was lie. was very likely to give rise to charges of this kind, and. be strongly recommended that gentlemen in the inter-. eats of the next candidate not to become an agent dur- ing the election. The petition must be dismissed„ and, it must be dismissed with costs, except asto the costa of the attendance of Mr. Tunstall, who had certainly ina some measure to thank himself for his position.
