, . . ; The tide THERE: is .au article-. in the last i of .. issue of the "• Edinburgh Review" , 'Enligriath' which gives much valuable and iniersting information with regard to the great., stream of emigration which is always issuing from European countries. . The English, it would ap, peM-, are still the great colonising people, though 1 every year there is an increase in the numbers of the*Gerraans, the Scandinavians, and the Italians, and, indeed, of nearly every European nation- ality, Who . seek to improve their fortunes by emigrating. During the thirty-seven year from 1853 to 1889, 3,439,138 English, 689,705 Scotch, Mid 2,775,007 Irish have Mt this country, chic) y for America. It is calculated that every year no / fewer than 130,000 Germans leave their ' natiVe' land, and -- to these Scandinavia adds anothet 62,000- and Italy, 32,000., Strange and inexpli- cable theugh it May appear, Belgium, one Of the most densely populated of European countries, is the only one which has a larger influx than efflux of population. The United States oar by far the largest number of these emigrants. Ninety-six per cent. of the Germans go there, and so do most of the Irish,but the Scdtch show a con- , siderable predilection for Canada. Many of the 'd Wiss go to South America, and about two-thirds 1 o the Italians settle in the coantries bordering on tie River Plate and Brazil.. The if •i . , I 1 titish are, however, pretty conspicuous in most i the. The Itlncorn Tonio Sol-fa. Choir surpassed all (their previous efforts in their performance if Han- del's "Judas Siaccahmos," on Monday evening, and Imany of the " critics" present acknowledged that 111 they had enjoyed a rich musical treat. The choir ave certainly enhanced their reputation, and both members and conductor are to be congratulated upon their well-deserved success. . ,

" - For the present, the negotiations between tile Town Council and the Ship Canal Company, res- eCting the company's application_ for a loan of .£150,000 from Warrrngton, are at en end. At tiny rate they will not be renewed with a view to any action being taken during the coming session 01 Parliament. This decision was arrived at. on Mon- day evenimy. at a special meeting of the Council held at the Town Ilall. The chief reason the Coy poration have rejected the proposition is that they could not agree with the Company upon the terms of the loan, it was unanimously felt by the mem- bers of the Council that to grant the loan without being allowed to decide the manner of its expendi cure would be doing an injusticP to the ratepay,:i.,. They suggested to the Company that. they should be allowed discretionary power in the handling of the ban, which should only be spent upon the local parts of the canal, especially the docks. Th • Company could offer no specific terms in this direc- tion, and as the period for applying for the borrow- ing powers was already very short, the Corporation decided to close the negotiations, until the Sid} Canal Company could make -a more favourable offer.

TRIBUTE OF THE LIBERAL PARTY. At the annual meeting of the members of the Liberal Mb on Monday evening, the Chairman Mr. .1. U. Fleminst, LP., proposed the following vote of condolence to the family of the deceased.—" i hat the Members of the Warrington Liberal Club, in Annul Meeting assembled, have heard with the most profound regret 01 the death of Mr. John 'Walker, and while placing upou record their high appreciation of his personal integrity, and unswerving devotion to the best interests of all classes of the community, would at the same time tender to Mrs. Walker and her *family their deepest sympathy in the sad bereavement which has overtaken them, and in the irreparable loss which they have sustained." Councillor Roberts, in aeconding the resolution, said that he did not wish to dwell on the qualities of Mr. Walker. Everyone present must be as well aware of them as he was, but he did not think that they would be just to themselves or to his memory unless they passed the resolution in the terms read by the President. Not only had the party sustained a great loss, but the town and.neighbourhood. He became ac- quainted with Mr. Walker. soon after he entered War- rington. For some time past Mr. Walker had beet, working with a full knowledge that he was possessed oh a disease which must in a few years at the most prove his death. But with this knowledge lie took on himself business engagements which must have paralysed many a harder and stronger man. In the face of that he never shrank from discharging any publie' duty. Not only bad the club lost a personal friend, but the town had lost a public man whose devotion was enly equalled by his fidelity to any case he undertook Mr. Walker was a near neighbour of his for a shorn time, and rarely did a day pass without their holding converse. Mr. Walker was most uncomplaining.. lb always tried to find an excuse for any bitterness wlibili might crop up even amongst the best of them. If he cculd find a good side to a case he would try to make others see it. He lent himself without stint to servo the cause of the people ainoegat whom ke dwelt and loved so well. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Plumpton supported the resolution, and aid that soon after Mr. Walker arrived in the town, he ,00k up his abode near him, and in his conversations tnd dealings with him lie had always found him to be a perfect gentleman. Be was consistent, and a friend on whom any man could rely. He was one to whom anyone could trust a secret. Not only had they lost a 'friend but they had lost a champion in the Liberal cause He was one whom it would be difficult to replace. (Applause.) Mr. Birchall said that the demise (a- tia public man had affected him more than that of Mr. Walker. He was always ready to do everything he could for anyone who invoked his aid. He never spared himself, and when they reflected on his weak condition under ordi- nary circumstances it was amazing to consider how he had laboured for the public good, apart from his ordi-,

, The most important event of the past week h. been the decision of the Board of Commissioners t( purchase the undertaking of the Runcorn Water- works Company. There will not be two opiniout• held that the water supply should be under the con- trol of the local authority. The misfortune is that our Commissioners of the past did not take the step which those of the present acting for the public weal have thought it wise and necessary to take. and for which future generations will give them credit, if the present should not do so. Those qualified to judge state that the price, although large one, is a fair and reasonable one, and much below what public Boards in other parts of the country have had to pay. In Warrington the Col poration had to pay 30 years' purchase of the maxi mum dividend payable. The terms our Commia. sioners have err inge4 are niuch more favourable and, as every p..ecaution is being taken, by the em ploymeht acconntant and an engineer, to see that the limoicial and the in,mhanical portions ohi the concern are what they are reppesetved to be. lie ratepayers w Ii have a good bargain, while at he same t ice the shareholders; of the Company ar htaini ng a profit able return cn their investment. DEATH ( )F MR. JOHN WALKER.

We regret to have this week to record the death lof Mr. John Walker, editor and proprietor of this journal, which took place on Saturday morning. For several years past Mr. Walker has not enjoyed !robust health, and on various occasions he has been :confined to his house by attacks ot illness, which lwere, however, generalli:not of long duration, nor

of so severe -a ,chatacter as to prevent him from discharging at least part of his ordinary duties His last illness commenced just a little over three weeks before its fatal termination, and was due to Bright's disease, a disorder from which Mr. Walker bad been a sufferer for about fourteen years. Almost from the commencement of the illness it was feared that, although lie had the assiduous attentions of Dr. White,there was but a slight hope if his recovery ; yet, notwithstanding his weaknest and suffering, Mr. Walker retained all his ment
talb

deftness till ibe end. Mr. Walker was born at Blackburn on the 29th of October, forty-seven years ago. He was the sop of a Blackburn man, Mr. Edward Walker, who was desciibed by one who knew him well as a staunett defender ot his class, independent in thought, and thoroughly upright in conduct. The deceased commenced his active life as a clerk in a Blackburn mill, but he soon began to show a literary gift, and this being observed by Mr. Ernest King, the former proprietor of the Blackburn " Timer," Mr. Walker was taken ,from the mill to the newspaper office. He sneers- nvely became junior reporter, and chief reporter, inci from that rose to the position of sub-editor, Ind Manager, and to that of literary contributor te ;he Preston ‘• Guardian" and the Blackburn "Times." Of his career in Blackburn we cannot give a bettei account 01111 ,in the words of Mr... IV. A. Abram, F.H.S., formerly editor of the Bliickburn "Times,' which were spoken at, a complimentary dinner 3,iven to Mr. Walker at Blackburn, at the time ol ;is removal to Warrington. Mr. Abram at that time ,and, " Mr. Walker had net limited his services to this professional duties—he had been to the fore in lalmnst everything that had teen going on in th. "WO during a /ong seriea of years. As a writei . the 'dialed, he had published sketcher, both on political and 'non-political Etiltet, that 'r thuiti point, shrewdness, and native wit Wt well Veortli to rank with similar writings of Edwin Waugh, coo Ben Brierley. He had also written poetry of e high class, while his contributions to the local pantomime always contained a great deal of 'wit, Litid a larger proportion of vocal puns than war usual in such matter. Mr. Walker had great abi- lity as a public speaker and debater. Not.only ha ee done great services on the platform, hut he took 1, leading position in the Blackburn Parliam •ntery. Debating Society, and in that arena inspired the confidence of his political friends, and the respect of his political opponents. The word " Reformer" would represent as truly as any single word couln to Mr. Walker's poeition,not only in regard to poli- tical but in regard to social uffaire. He hail been characterised by thoroughness in his opiniona,•and he never flinched from upholdine his principles. On all occasions Mr. Walker had .ii.h (leateti the rights of the pecple and self-governineet, again; monopoly and sectarian ascendancy." Mr. Walker was for some lime a , inember• of the Elackburn School Board and in that position he strongly ad- vocated the rights of the people to self-government. -id resisted to the extent of his powers all at- kkempta to establish sectarian ascendancy. It should be mentioned too, that Mr. Walker's journalistic eareer included a residence in London where he was for two years engaged upon the "Sun" series of newspapers, part of the time as night editor. He kvas also for a period on the slat/ of the " Con- slnental Herald." Mr. Waika. removed from lilecal..r; to War- rington about eight years ago,to undertake the edit- trrhip of the Examiner.' At t•let end ^f twelyel months he went into partnership wii :dr. John roulmin, tie then proprietor 'of: this paper, the business being carried on under the, name of John Walker end Company. At the eud f,naother two years Mr. Toulmin retired and, Mr. Walker became sole proprietor. In addition to his editorial work the deceased gentleman, as is well known in! Warrington,.took •an active interest in a varlet: of public questions; Being a fluent and forci- ble speaker he was a valuable end helpful ally in the public advocacy of any question. Upan Liberal platforms he was a frequent and always a. vigorous and acceptable speaker, and there we rarely a public meeting for the furtherance of thk temperance caws at 'which he was not present, when not prevented by illness or absence from the. rown. Alike by pen and tongue he furtheredi many local movements. He was the chief initia- tor of the agitation for the freeing of tht librar, and the zeal and energy which he threw' into that cause have met with a reward which was highly acceptable to him—a free library and a greatly extended use of the books gathered together there. lie was an untiring advocate of' sanitary reform, and on more then one occasion lie made special efforts to strengthen the arms those who are anxious to make the town as im

TIIE FUNERAL. • The remains of the deceased were interre .1 at Black- burn Cemetery, on Wednesday. The funeral cortege left the late Mr. Walker's rcsidence, at Latchford, iaf ter a short service, conducted by the Rev. John Yonge, shortly after eleven clock, and proceeded slowly along the Knutsford-road a Bank Quay Station. PrecedingP the hearse was a procession of close upon 100 mourners, composed Al deputations from the Liberal Association, the Liberal Club, the Temperance Federation, Independent Order etl Rechabites, the Warrington Labour Party, the Institute of Journalists, the Starr-Bowkett Society. Followin the hearse came coaches containing the following mourners :—Mrs. Walker, Mr. E. V. Walker (sos), Mis C. Walker (daughter), Mrs. Cadman (is t er-in-law), Mr. B. Sandford (brother-in-law), Mrs. Henry Roberts. there were also coaches from Councillor F. Monks, tr. R. Davies. Among those who formed the procession w( re the Rev., John Yonge (Congregational Minister), the Rev. J.' Varley (Latchford Baptist Minister), t 7 itincilf,trs 11 nne.

Fleming,J.P.,G.Plumpton, ape.; Messrs. William Roberts (Sec. of the Temperance 'ederation), John Podmore (of the I. 0. R.), A. H. Lee, Gandy, J. Titchett, S. li. Stringer, J. Ellison, J. Mountield, T. Birchall, J.P., Samuel Wright, J.P., Charles Jackson Holmes, George Wallington, William! G. Clay, J. S Garland,R. Bennett, Jones, J. Mitchell, J. Clayton, Thomas Malkin, G. Gilks, J Hartley, John Shaw Green, T. ilawtl.orn. Jame: Corradine, Z. Armitage, Albinson, William Bibby, T. IPrie-tman, Hickman, W illiam Lon.csliaw. Jas. 14.1vans,' land James Strange ; also the following menitrers of the " Examiner " staff t—Messrs. H. Bond, T. Ward, J. E. A. Lake ; Messrs. Lunt and G. Grundy 'represented the Warrington"Guardian,"and Mr.C.Lyons, ! the local branch of the Institute of Journalists. As the solemn procession wended its course along the route, signs of respect and sorrow, at the demise of the deceased were plentiful. The blinds in many house windows, and in almost all office windows, were drawn. Alter crossing Warrington Bridge, the procession pro- ceeded past Arpley Station, and along Wilson Patten-st. to Bank (pay Station. Upon arriving here the proces- sion dispersed. The coffin was conveyed to the Blackburn train, by which the principal mourners left shortly after twelve o'clock. At Blackburn station the funeral party were met by a representative body of Mr. Walker's relariv and friends, and numerous addi- tional wreaths were laid upon the coffin. A procession, including six mourning coaches and some private carri- ages was again formed and proceeded to the Blackburn Cemetery, where an impressive funeral service was con- ducted by the Rev. A. Forster and the Rer.F.L. Shilitoe, Congregational ministers. The coffin was one of finely polished oak, with brass fittings, and on the brass plate was the following. inscription :—"John Walker, Died November 12th, 1892,aged 47 years." It should be added that the funeral arrangements were in the hands of Mr., Mounfield, of Buttermarket-st., Warrington.

The Rev. John Yonge writes us with reference to Mr. Walker as follows :--'• I should like to put on record a brief, but cordial expression of my esteem and reaard for the late Mr. John Walker. His death, at the early iage, comparatively, of 47, is greatly to be regretted, not

only by his wide circle of personal friends, but by all, 'iwho are interested in political and social reforms. To. the full extent of his time and opportunity, Mr. Walker was devoted and enthusiastic in the advocacy and pro- motion of every scheme and policy which make for righteousness, and which tend to the progress of human well-being. In these columns, there is no need for rx to dwell upon his ardent and intelligent Liberalism : for he has made the Examiner the continual vehicle of his. thought upon all the political projects of the day. More-1 over, he was always ready to give utterance in public to his political opinions, and in doing so he proved that he had a great gift of free and forcible public address. What, however, I would more spcciallv desire to dwellt upon, is the spirited and unselfish way in which he ever espoused the cause of temperance. Many men, and many journalists, rather tight shy of any emphatic,: Pronouncement upon this subject, bet it 51t..u1d affect! their standing in commerce, or raise a prejudice againso their newspaper. I have been grieved and chagrinned many times by the selfish cowarjice of men who profess ardent attachment to the cause temperance, but wh, shirk all prominent identification with it, lest it should affect their business. Mr. Walker had not a grain of this selfishness in his whole cump,sition. What hel believed to be right, lie fearlessly advocated, and never' thought how nis doing so might alfeet himself. • His death has thus t% ade a breach in the ranks of the tem- perance party in this town, which it will be very difficult to fill.

" Tomperance,however,waa not the only social reform] in which Mr. Walker was interested, and in which he ever stood ready to take his part. He would, I know, have engaged much more actively in social and philanthropic work, had it not been for the lack of physical strength. Indeed, it is amr rvel to me that lie did so much as he did. Few men could be braver or more courageous than he. It takes an heroic fortitude .-.c) work on in the exacting toils of journalism as Mr. Walker did, with the inward knowledge that a fatal disease is working its deadly will from year to year. I ;hall alwa3s hold him in honourable recollection as a man of high conscientiousness and unselfish devotior to duty. Loving devotion to his family, loyal fidelit:i o the cause to which he had given uk intelligent advocacy and support, kept him :taunchly at his post. He was far more than a merely professional journalist. I do not think he -.;ould ever have edited a Conservative journal as som, have done, while personally holding Liberal opinions He was far too honest and thorough so to sink hi, manhood in his profession. And hence he leave behind him an untarnished record, and an example of it;?rsititent adherence to conviction that is highly, " Henceforth,another must fill his editorial chair, and rake in hand the Editor's pen ; but I doubt if Liberalism, temperance, and social reform in Warrington will easily or ever find a truer servant, or a better advocate than he who has just passed out of mortal sight." ;

LETTERS OF CONDO...ENCE. 52, Fitzwilliam Square, Dublin, Nov. 14, 1892. Dear Mrs. Walker,— May I be permitted to convey to you my heart- felt sympathy in your great affliction? The news of your husband's death fell upon me with a great shock. In my short connection with Warrington, I had learned to respect and admire him more than I can easily des- :Tibe. The life of high and holy purpose the heart of perfect singleness, the talents that were always devoted to the good of others, the cheerful sacrifice of self, all ;hese things even a brief and casual acquaintance with him enabled me to perceive. One can in sonic degree ippreciate what his loss must mean to you and his little ,mes, when one knows what his loss will be to the com- munity among whom he lived and laboured. Be has not lived in vain. His example and his work • will bear ;ood fruit long after those who knew him have passed away. But it will be hard to fill the vacant place that he has left among his fellow-citizens and friends. They will mourn for him with a sorrow only less keen than that which you will feel. Praying that God may com- fort your widowed heart, ' Believe me, Yours faithfully. no ivizero mod , ARTHUR HOUSTON.

Under the auspices of this society a three days' itemperance crusade has just been carried out in 'Runcorn. Since the League was commenced in the town about four years ago, much good has been laccomplishe.d amongst the Catholic portion of the population, and the organisation is now in a pros- perous condition, controlled by a set of energetic officers and committee. Mr. Clynch is president. and Mr. Quinn secretary. With the object of bring- ing more people within the scope of its influence. Mr.-Richard Collins. of Manchester, was engaged to deliver a course of lectures in the Catholic school at Mill Brow. . The first lecture was delivered on Friday evening last week under the presidency of the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, who described how he formed the League with only five members, and now they numbered 300 mem- bers besides children. He thanked God that the League had now attained such a firm and successful footing. The principal, speaker of course, was Mr. Collins, who it may he interesting to know has attained the patriarchs' age of 82 years. Although he has the hoary head,whit_ is-said to be a crown of glory, yet he is as straight and sprightly as many a man at fifty.and his voice is power- ful and deep-toned, and he speaks for nearly an hour without anv appearance of distress. Mr. Collins took the pledge 50 years ago from the saintly Father Matthew, and since that timehe has been an earnest, persistent, and consistent advocate of temperance, both indoors and outdoors ; and .he - has delivered many thousand addresses. During his,three days' stay in Runcorn he delivered four speeches, and all were cliaraeterised by trenchant argument, Caustic wit, at:d Irish humour. The best attended trieuting was on Sunday night,' when the schoolroom was crowded to excess, and Mr. Collins cave his celebrated " loaf lecture," and at the conclusion -nearly forty persons tcok the pledge in the solemn form prescribed by the League. On Sundae afternoon a successful meeting was held In Bt. -John's Weston, with the highly gratifying result that a number of persons took the pledge, and a branch of the League was formed and officers were appointed. During his crusade Mr. Collins has been ably assisted by the Pastor. the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. B. Bisbrown, T. Le, T. Cooke, Councillor Williamson (Birkenhead), Houghton (Warrington), Clynch, and Quinn, and the results have been very satisfactory. It is expected that Mr. Collins will pay another visit to the town in the near future.

Supper was partaken of, and subsequently Mr.- Parry moved, and Mr. W. Wright seconded, a vote of thanks to the ladies who had kindly looked after the tea. This closed the proceedings,) and the members dispersed, after having spent a most enjoyable evening.

. . PONERAL OF MR. JAMES RIOBY.—On Saturday the re- nains of Mr. James Rigby, of Belle Monte, Frodsham, were interred in the graveyard connected with the iParisli Church, Overton. The funeral was of a purely n-ivate character. The deceased gentleman, who died n Thursday, at theadvanced age of 81 years, was the m of Mr. George Rigby, who filled the position of 5 instable and other offices, in the Frodsham district, for any years. Mr. Rigby for a long period efficiently ~' ~erformed the duties of managing director of the Nes- , ton Colliery Company. After leaving there he came to - Frodsham, where he joined 14 cousin' the late Mr.Rigby ' - Pickering, in the corn Mills gt. Frodshara Bridge. He retired from the partnership some years ago. He was the member of an old Lancashire landed family at New- L't burgh, near Orruskirk. He was a Churchman, and a tuncli Conservative, but he never took any prominent itt in political affairs. H 9 leaves seven children to ,t ourn his death. rhe deceased was held in high esteem • ,- an extensive circle of friends. PAROCHIAL COMMTTTEEL—At the monthly meeting of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Com- iittees held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday vening—present : • Mr A. Thomas, J.P., chairman; IDr. Robinson, Messrs. H. E. Heywood, J. Moseley IWilliams, T. Lewis, T. Davies, H. Tiley, R. Bate, and Colonel Ashton, clerk—the Clerk reported that Messrs. ',naming were progressing very favourably with the .ring for water, having got to a depth of about 80 feet, the water rising to within four feet of the surface, and that they purposed going to the full depth of 300 feet, this being the depth arranged for, as they anticipated a purer quality of water from that depth, as well as a larger quantity, and the proposal of the contractors was approved.—A letter was read from Mr. R, G. Carpenter, of Hillsboro', calling the attention of the committees to the unsatisfactory state of the main sewer at Overton. A long discussion ensued as to the best means of remedy- ing the evil complained of, and it was decided to consult with the Medical Officer of Health.—The committees then decided to visit the several sewerage outfalls with- in their district on Saturday neat.

I'm told that there is some hitch between the leaders ,of the two ,political parties in town, respecting the vacancy for St. John's Ward, caused y. the elevation of Councillor Blackhurst to an • •Idermanic seat. When the • deputation from the parties met before the Ist of November, and corn- ! omised respecting the municipal elections, it was . treed by both parties that each should have the wer to return unopposed, two aldermen, and that in the event of either party making a selection from the ranks of the councillors, that party should ": lbe allowed to fill the vacancy so caused. This was 1. only right and fair; and it formed a phase in the corn- : /promise that could not very well have been over- ; looked. Still it is this that lam told the Conserva= Lives wish to overlook, for they dispute having '.71 entered into any such ageeement, and are prepar- ing to fight the ward. This is to be regretted if it is meant as a political stratagem, for although in politics we Liberals deem ourselves advanced,either our lack of alertness—or our scruples—prevent us from gaining a point in the way in which our : friends of the •" integrity of the Empire," pro- to achieve one. c. ,

It is a common thing for the prisoners at the dorougb Court to be frustrated in their ingenious , devices to avert the fall of the sword of justice. . But it is rarely that our borough magistrates are ' frustrated in their little devices. Yet this is an in- - stance which was both " heard and seen" on Sun- day, when a great portion of the magisterial body betook themselves to the Parish Church. The d ivine service was ended, and as the last strains of the organ were gradually dying among the ancient .isles, the J.P.'s walked with stately mien until , , within the protection of a solitary shelter which : 'shall be nameless. Then they delibArated among J ithemselves upon the ways and means of allowing a : certain labour magistrate to always find himself at ! court alone. They were much perturbed at this horny-handed son of toil claiming his share of the pie of honour, and they felt that a little "boycot- ting," would be an effective way of killing his am- bition to administer justice. The question arose as ' to what day this Mr. "Labour Man" would attend . ,court. Some said one day, and some said another,. , I soon a tierce and earnest debate occurred.

-- And it was in the midst of this wordy war that , certain member of the Bench, for the first time poke. He said he could throw some light upon the subject, and the gathering crowded round with eager faces. • lie knew something they said, for he ~prefaced his remarks with that indication of ,levity, a grin and a wink. Then he said " friends, don't wrangle. I is of no use. I know it isn't. I met Mr." Labour Man 'yesterday, and he told me- • "Ali 1 What was it.r mine the unanimous •query "Oh, well, he said he really had so nixeh time lon his hands that he thought he'd attend court, every day." Every magistrate then remembered an. sngagerneut he had to keep at 12.30. Speaking of magistrates reminds me of a peculiar- • ;suggestion that 1 believe was made to the magis- trates attending court on Monday. After the pub- lic business had been transacted it was suggested - that in all licensing cases which Were not of a heinous description, stirvild be referred to the Watch Committee ; and also that the Watch Coin- • . mittee should adjudicate upon the cases Privately.- ' This may have been meant as a joke upon the new ,megistrates or it may not.- Suffice it to say it was.. Sdisrnissed instantly ; but it impressed upon those who had only just flashed their judicial swords, the., leet ssity to heed the expressive words of a moth•rn ;otriposition, • " always keep your peepers wide il.vake." The suggestion was so-palpably "off-side," that comments are needless.

- - James Wood was charged at the Warrington Borough FDlice Court,on Monday morning,defacing a fence in the Park, on the 29th ulc., by inscribing thereon certain ob- jectionable figures. The assistant park keeper proved the case, and said the fence was that dividing the boys' and girls' gymnasium. On witness catshing him com- mitting the offence, he ran away, and witness ran after him and caught him and got a constable to obtain his address. He summoned him, but be did not appear,and warrant was issued, and he was apprehended that morning.—Ths prisonerliaid he had rubbed off the figures. but this was denied. After being severely rebuked by Alderman Harrison, the prisoner was fined 51.aad costs, Us. in all.

The few people in Court on Tuesday morning almost unanimously smiled when they heard of how Catherine Brown was conveyed right from Warrington Bridge to Horsemarket-street, the previous night. She may have been need to better things in her time, or she may not. But she is certainly very expecting and extravagant. She was going home after getting drunk on Tuesday night, and when she arrived at the Bridge, she said to the policeman in a dreamy tone "Lemma lie down 'ere, my (hie) legs wana sit (bin) downer." No she wouldn't get up. She obstinately persisted in spoiling her goose- berry coloured dress, by slumbering in the gutter. So P.C. Delahay had to drive her down to the Mansion in that beautiful Government equipage, sometimes called a.handcart. She stayed at the Idanaion all night, and not having 10s. about her the next morning, the Bench seat her,at Government expenas,to try a change of air at Strangeways, for a fortnight.
IT WAS ALL FIIDON.

A man's name and his actions are soinetlmvs synony- mous in literal construction. This was so with the case of a man,who looked like a "Yank," and who boasted a strong goatbeard, and a broken arm, and lay about the dock, at the Warnngton Police Court, on Wednes- day, in an aimless fashion. His name was Charles Fudge. A constable said that on the Oth of October, Charles popped his head out of a door in Bakehouse- yard, and cried for help. When the officer got to the house, there was no aound whatever, save the strains of the song " Charley is my Darling," or something else, being sung in lullaby tones. So the officer resumed the tenor cf his 'teat ; but, in a few moments Charley's goat- beard protruded from the door, and his voice was raised in a pitiful supplication for help. With rapid stride, the policeman slid for the house again. Silence again predominated with supremacy, and it was after noise- less meditation that" Bobby" came to the firm and unmovable conviction that it was all fudge. This con- viction was confirmed when Charles Fudge's beard again issued from the door. The policemen said to it " I will report you," and then from behind the goat beard, could be heard the silvery tones of Charley. "Then the divil take ye for a spalpeen." A summons was sent to Fudge's house the next daT. He went out. He didn't say why, at the time, but it was evidently for the pur- pose of breaking his arm, because he told the Bench he li. had no other reason for leaving home so suddenly. They said " It's all fudge, you will be fined ss. and costs." He paid.

THE New 141AGISTRATBS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning Councillor H. Roberts subscribed to the usual delaration and took his seat as a magistrate. Mr. P. Davies said he congratulated the new magistrates on their presence there that morning, and expressed the hope that in one way the business of that court would be conducted better than it had been before, that was that they would have the magistrates present at the time that they were wanted. He was sure nearly every advocate in the town had been very greatly incon- venienc,ed by having to wait for the attendance of magistrates. One gentleman he must compliment, Alderman Harrison, who was always there to the minute, but others who had themselves appointed, he supposed, the mest convenient days on which to be pre- sent, and therefore ought to fulfil their engagements, were often absent when they were wanted. It would be a very great convenience to the advocates and all concerned if they would attend punctually on the days on which they promised to be there. He was sure the new magistrates would be a very great acquisition to the Bench, if it was only in point of convenience in tran- sacting the business, but in other ways he was satisfied, they would be a great acquisition.—The Town Clerk, who had attended the court to prosecute in a meat case, in which Mr. Davies appeared to defend, but which WWI withdrawn without having been entered into, said he entirely endorsed the remarks made by his friend.—Mr. Councillor Roberts said as one of the new magistrates he thanked the gentlemen who had spoken. He hoped be and the other new members of the Bench would deserve the kind things said that morning.

SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, W. G. Gooch, W. Mitchell, and T. H. Pearson. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON WARRINGTON BAILIFFS.—MichaeI Flanaghan, (son) and Annie Flanaghan, (mother) of Vitriol Square,Earlestown, were charged with assaulting Wm. H. Once, Faulkner, and Burrows, bailiffs of the Warrington County Court. Mr. A. Browne, Warrington, prosecuted on behalf of the Treasury Department of the County Courts Department, and Mr.R. Stuart defended. The female defendant was charged with assaulting rice and Burrows, and the male defendant with assault- ing Grice and Faulkner. At the outset Mr. Stuart took objection to the proceedings on the ground that the bailiffs bad committed a trespass, inasmuch as the house was not the house of the defendant in the County Court under which the distress was levied, as also the furniture, and that therefore the bailiffs being trespassers, the defendants were entitled to protect their own goods, and to do everything necessary to prevent the goods from being taken away.—Mr. Browne replied that the defen- dants did not pay the money under protest. The course the defendants ought to have pursued was to have paid the money under protest, hnd then to have inter- pleaded by entering into the usual bonds in the r,ounty Court and having the action tried beforti the 'ridge in the County Court. Mr. Browne also quoted the ease of Regina v. Briggs, which decided that justices of the peace could not decline jurisdiction on the ground

that a question might arise as to an execution under a process of a court of justice. On these grounds Mr. Browne submitted that Mr. Stuart's argument was bad.—The court over-ruled Mr. Stuart's objection.— From the facts adduced by the prosecution it appeared that on the 4th inst. the three bailiffs accompanied by another one named Gardener were sent by the High Bailiff to execute a distress upon the goods of Michael Flanaghan,at Vitriol-square, Earlestown. On their arri- val at the house of the defendants, they were informed by the male defendant that the house was his, and in support of that statement ha prcduced the rent book, on which the word "junior" had been added to Michael Flanaghan, the male defendant's father. The head bailff pointed out that the addition had been written in ink of a different colour to the first. The bailiff also tried to induce the defendant to pay the amount of the sum in respect of which the warrant was issued, viz., Ms. odd. The defendants, however, refused to pay, and threatened that there would be bloodshed if the bailiffs attempted to remove any goods. They also said that it would be a worse job for the bailiffs than the last one at Barlestown, evidently referring to a recent case tried at the Warrington Petty Sessions, •wherein the defendant was sentenced to one month's imprisonment for assaulting a bailiff. Notwithstanding the threats, Grine went for a pony and trap, and on returning with Faulkner they found the two defendants standing at the door. The male defendant had a stick in his hand, and the female had a strap, the upper por- tion of which was wrapped round her wrist. Both were standing in a threatening attitude. Gardner requested the defendants to retire from the house, but the male said that he would not. Grine thereupon shoved him on one side. The defendant immediately struck him across the head with his stick, and was about to renew the assault when Faulkner came to his assistance, and pulled the aggressor into the street. The female defendant fol- lowed Grine, and struck him with the buckle end of the strap, and seizing him by the waistcoat pulled off every button. She also tore his shirt front, and hit him in the eye with her fist. The Bench, after hearing the evi- dence, came to the conclusion that a serious assault had been committed, and fined the defendants £2 4s. each.

Thaler Fame TIM MARICHT.—James Clark was charged with stealing threepence from the stall of Leo Lewin, a Jew, in the Market Place, on Saturday evening. The Chief Constable said about half-past lie on the evening mentioned, the prisoner came to the stall and bought a pennyworth of Wray, then said he was going to have something more, and putting his hand into the cash bowl, took out three pennies. The complainant objected, and he said "That threepence belongs to me, and I am going to have it," and abused Lewin very much. P.C. Roper was brought, and took him into custody.—The complainant, who took the usual Jewish oath, with his hat on, corroborated this statement.—The complainant said he tasted the toffey and spat it out not liking it, and told the prosecutor it was not fit to eat, and he would have his penny back. He put his hand into the bowl, and thought he only took out a penny, but got hold of three pennies.—The prisoner was fined ss. TIMIDAY.—Before Messrs. Fancy Quiwit Ito...tn.—The boy, Percy Quinn, 11 years of age, who has gained celebrity as a market thief, was charged with stealing a quantity of sweets , and other things from the shop Of Mr. S. Lawless, I grocer, Mark, t Place. The evidence showed that the I boy was found at dark the previous night in Mr. Lawless's shop enjoying a kind of a pic-nic on a small scale. The scale was one used for weighing tea in, and Percy had filled it with a quantity of sweets and jam, which he was eating with relish. The jam had been extracted from six different jars. The bogs previous character was reviewed, and the Bench concluded that it was melan- choly case. Enquiries were made about the child's parents, and Inspector Uphill of the R.S.P.C.C., said he had visited their house in Pilkington's Yard, and found that they were respectable, with a clean house, and plenty of food in it for the boy if he liked it. Mr. Bunt, the Chief Constable, said" Well, his parents have altered very much lately,and if the Inspector's statement is correct, I fancy it is the constant attention of the police which has brought that change about." The boy was committed for 14 days' imprisonment, after which he will ge to a reformatory school tor five years. - - -

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

FATALITY AP WESTON POINT. On Wednesday afternoon. Wm. Hignett, aged 15 years, was killed on the Ship Canal works, at Weston Point. Hignett was employed as a labourer, and he was coup- ling up a number of waggons which had been loaded with soil by a steam navvy, when a number of other waggons were sent along the line, and collided with the stationary waggons. The deceased was caught be- tween the buffers and crushed to death instantly.

div.head: BIG VESSEL AT SALTPORT.
div.p: A BIG VESSEL AT SALTPORT.

The owners of the se. Helen, 4,700 tons, now dis- charging at Saltport, have decided to load her with general cargo for Havana and Santiago de Cuba. Goods will be received from her at Manchester and Saltport during the early part of next week. The steamer ar- rived on Sunday and passed up the ten miles of the canal to Saltport in two hours, in charge of Mr. Hodgson, one of the Liverpool pilots, having entered the canal on one of the lowest tides of the year. The wash from her propeller scarcely reached the banks, and it has now been demonstrated that the canal is navigable in perfect safety by large vessels. The as. Berlin commenced dis- charging at 8 axe. on Friday last, and delivered 1,100 tons of farina, returning down by the canal an Monday, without a pilot.

div.head: SALFORD'S AID TO THE CANAL.
div.p: SALFORD'S AID TO THE CANAL.

The Town Council of Salford on Monday resolved to promote in Parliament a bill authorising the Corporation to lend £1,000,000 to the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany. In reply to questions, the Town Clerk stated that although the Corporations of the city and borough and the Canal Company were going forward with separato bills, these bills when they got into Committee were almost sure to be consolidated.

div.head: MEETING OF SALFORD RATEPAYERS. THE LOAN NEGATIVED.
div.p: MEETING OF SALFORD RATEPAYERS. THE LOAN NEGATIVED.

A meeting of the ratepayers of Salford, convened by the Mayor, was held on Wednesday evening for the pur- pose of assenting or otherwise to the promotion of a bill In Parliament authorising the Corporation to lend a million sterling to the Manchester Ship Canal Company for the completion and equipment of the undertaking. The meeting was not very large. The resolution autho- rising the loan was defeated by a considerable majority. The Mayor (Alderman Keevney) thereupon demanded a poll of the ratepayers. hiAIiCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE CANAL. £2,000,100 MORE TO BE LENT.

A special meeting of the Manchester City Council on Wednesday, without comment or discussion, passed a formal resolution empowering the Corporation of Man- chester to render further financial assistance to the Manchester Ship Canal. The additional amount is £2,000,000. Another bill was also approved to acquire land for wharves, slaughter-houses, and lairages, with a view o! slaughtering cattle at Mode Wheel instead of Birkenhead. A public meeting, convened by the Mayor, in response to a requisition, was subsequently held to confirm or otherwise the resolution. They Mayor moved the confirmation of the resolution. Sir J. Harwood, in seconding, said they were asking £2,000,000, but if Sal- ford provided £1.000,000 then Manchester would only spend £1,000,000 of the £2,000,000 asked for. The sale of surplus land and of plant as asset.s. would reimburse the Council to some extent, so the outlook was not so bad as made out. It was estimated that a saving would , be effected of £61,400 to the citizens if nothing else were done but the erection of the slaughter-house by the Markets Committee as approved by the Council. The ! resolution was adopted.

ST. MARY'S •. PARISH CHGRCH, (WARRINGTON JUNIOR Lgeons.—Played on the ground of the former on Satur- day, before a fair number of spectators. The home team mustered strongly, whilst their opponents had to deplore the absence of Miller and Howard. During the first half the visitors played with the wind, but this seemed no advantage, for the Saints, playing strongly, had the best of the game, and it was not long before threadgold ran over, no goal resulting. The home team still continued to have the best of it until half-time, but no addition to the score was made. The second half saw a complete change comae over the game, for the visitors worked with a will, and, outstaying the homesters, pressed them severely, and Garrity, securing from a scrimmage near the line, dodged his men in fine style, and scored, Carey giving his side the lead by landing the goal. This suc- cess was greeted with cheers by the visitors' followers, and towards the close the excitement was intense, each team striving hard to increase their score. Nothing, however, resulted from the efforts on either side, and at the end of a well-fought game the score stood as—Parish Church, one goal (five points) ; St. Mary's, one try (two points). WARRINGTON RANOHRS Y. PRMIIHRTON "A" TRAM.— Played at Pemberton. The Rangers won the toss, and took advantage of the slope and wind. The opening stages found the game in the visitors' 25, until Massey relieved by punting well in touch. From the line-out, Pemberton broke away, and Gasket] kicked dead. Upon the drop out the Rangers, by smart passing, took the I oval into their oppononents* quarter, where, after a series of scrimmages, Clarke got away, and throwing over to ' Clare, that player dropped a capital goal for Warrington. Not to be denied, the visitors again pressed, and after s strong forward rush to the line, Clarke smartly picked up and scored in a favourable position, the same player landing a goal from the place. After the interval, the borne forwards, headed by Nicholson and Whittle, burst away, and looked like scoring, when Ashton saved daringly. The homesters hereabout severely tested the Rangers' defence, Winstanley and Blackburn almost scoring, but eventually Price brought about the much desired relief, by kicking finely in touch at centre. With the exception of a minor to each side, nothing further was scored, and the game ended, Rangers, 2 goals 1 minor; Pemberton, 2 minors.

WARSIINOTON A •. MOSSLIY A.—At Mossley. The home team, winning the toss. elicited to play uphill. Warrington kicking off were soon on the Mossley line, where • vigerous attack was made by the visiting for- wards, Lawless scoring within a few minutes. Ashurst'e return to the drop out left the game' in the home quer- ten, but the packs were relieved by Roberts and Taylor dribbling away, only to see Barnes nullify the effort by a capital bit of work. A couple of excellent displays ia passing by Warrington, in which Thornley,Smith, Lally, and Barnes were notable, gave Mossley air anxious time of it. The defence was too good, and the, danger cleared to the centre, but Ashurst returned the leather to the line. Again Roberts came away to midfield; but as quickly Barnes and Daniels, by some capital effort, changed the venue of the warfare to the home 25, where Moseley took advantage of a mull, their career not being stayed until the oval had reached the Warrington line. Bailey dribbled splendidly to half way, and in stopping a rush the home custodian got injured, and had to retire for the rest of the game. Further capital passing by the visit* backs placed their opponents' line ix jeopardy, and Smith and Lally getting the ball away to Lawless, this player effected a splendid run in, grounding dose te the poets, Barnes converting. Then Smith threw to Lally, who ran finely, but the final pass was not correct, Moseley escaping with a minor. The home team eould not clear their lines, some grand strong play by Newry and Davies forcing the back, until eventually the hone forwards rushed into the Warrington quarter. Lally made another fine run, but after Moseley had made an- other unsuccessful raid Daniels kicked down the field, and Glover, Bailey, and Lawless headed Warrington to the other end, the ball being kicked dead. Half time arrived with Warrington 1-1-2 to nil. Upon the resump- tion of the contest Messily for a time held the upper hand: until Newry, Higham, and Molyneux rushed to neutral territory. This episode was soon followed by another attack on the part of Mossley, until • long kick went dead. Lee almost got in after this; but Barnes, intercepting a pass ran finely to belt way, and Higham, Barrett, and Eden supplemented the effort by carrying the ball to the Mossley posts Here Lees tried to get away, a splendid tackle by Lawless ending his onward career. Directly afterwards Lally and Barnes manipulated the leather to Lawless, who, getting an opening, dashed splendidly over the line. A long kick by Danieli still found Mossley defend- ing ; but the defenders were in turn attackers, Warring- ted having to concede a minor after some tough scrim- mages on their line. The Warrington forwards, who , had been far superior to Mossley, again forced their I antagonists back, and while the game was raging in the visitors' quarters Lally passed to Lawless, who, after eluding several opponents, wound up a brilliant run three parts the length of the ground by scoring his fourth try near the poits. The pla..e kick failed. After this Bailey, Thornley, Highari, and Davies rushed into the home 2, where McAuley, getting clear away, had a capital chance of scoring, but were overtaken, only searing a minor, the game ending—Warrington 1----3"-3 to 0-0--3. WARRINGTON v. MOSSLEY.

Moseley have alwaya been favourites with Warrington audiences, but it was a wonder that, considering the dreadful state of affairs in the town, so large a" pt." assembled at Wilderspool on Saturday to witness the first match between these rivals this mum's. Both sides had good beams up for the occasion, there not being a single dissentient from the side which had been originally selected.

At 3.30 Moseley kieke,cl off towards the pavilion goal, and no reply being forthcoming, the Moesleyitee, at the first time of asking, caught an insight of the home goal. Jolley partially relieved, whilst a free kick taken by Fair. Turner improved Matters so much that half-way saw the game being contested. The pace was very fast and tbe several movements were worked so rapidlythat it requieed the strict attention of the ,keenest observer to follow the players. Some floe exchanges between Eagland and Boscow saw the latter in difficulties, but he was equal to the task, and a fine kick in close quarters beat his dangerous opponents back. Evans, Bate, and Plumpton, now passed beautifully, the latter being well held by Sheldon. Bate again initiated a passing move- ment, which led up to Turner putting in a fine run and kick past England, but Plumpton failed to get up in time and take advantage of what seemed a possible 1 dunce of scoring. Lorimer tackled Bate well, but a feint to pass by Evans saw him dodging finely, and when everyene had predicted a score, he came a crop- per near the line. Ashworth and Corscadden relieved slightly, whilst a free kick to Warrington taken by Turner was met by Ashworth running splendidly round his opponents, and placing the game again at neutral quarters. Webster had now a chance of distinguishing himself, and in co-partnership with Berry, Ashton, and Holmes, attacked once mere. Newby luckily kicked out of danger, and Boscow was reached, and the oval being in safe hands, a loud cheer greeted the home cut- todian's fine play. Mossley would not be denied, and beaded by their international, Ashworth and Newby, the home lines were assailed in a •igerous manner, and Lorimer ended the proceedings by forcing a minor. Both Turner and Webster exchanged kicks with Ragland, and then a good run and pass by Bandies to Plumpton saw the latter being tackled before he could get Into his stride. Berry led the home for- wards to the line, Sheldon saving daringly, and altheugh Ashworth again cleared, Boscow was to the fore with a judicious kick, and the Warringtonians were aggressors once more. The visitors now took advantage 1 some risky passing of the home backs, and the game was on the pavilion line in quick time, and F. Lorimer, 1 being in a good position, essayed a shot at gnat, the oval going on the outside—a very near shave. It was now the homesters' turn, for a run by Jolley saw him naming wildly to Holmes, and a glnrious chance lost. With the Mossley umpire suspended for gross infringe- ment, the Warrington men maintained the attack, and Nevins with one run brought forth ringing cheers. This last run led up to the home forwards rushing the oval over the line, and England saved. Again Jolley got clear, but failed in the finishing stroke, whilst tackling by Efeesom and Plumpton of several opponents stopped the Mossley men from relieving. Ashton now became prominent in a rush, whilst Webster ncar the call of half-time was running very strong, but nothing of note occurred, and the first half ended with no substantial score. On resuming Warrington were early en evidence, and some passing by Evans, Bate, Heesom, and Webster saw the lengthy three-quarter being pushed into touch near the quarter-flag. Some loose play now occurred, and Heesom kicking to F,agland, Plumpton exhi- bited a rare turn of speed, and beating the Manley back for pessession, he raced over for a brilliant try. With the kick at goal failing Ashworth dropped out, but this act had no sooner been done than Jolley picked up in the loose, and a tine effort realised a second try, barely a minute after its predecessor, Plumpton this time failing with the place. Ashton next tried sabot at goal from a mark, but it was a miserable attempt, and the visitors, still hopeful, plodded on, and some dribbling by Manson, Batley, and Newby, reached the Warrington lines for the last time, for a continuance of ecrimmages was followed by the Warrington backs taking the oval direct to their oppo- nents' line. Passing was here being indulged in, and Bate was the leading operator when he missed his footing somehow, and fell heavily. On being picked up it was found that he had sustained another fracture of the collar bone, and the popular player was at once taken to Liverpool, where the injured limb was attended to. Little interest was taken in the match after this, and the end was finally reached with the score Warrington, 0-2-2; Mossley, 0-0-2,

div.head: WIDNES v. ST. CLEMENT'S.
div.p: WIDNES v. ST. CLEMENT'S.

These teams met for the first time this stason, at Widnes to-day. The Rochdale club brought a strong team, and Widnes turned out as selected. Wharf started for St. Clement' at half past three, and Clarke let the visitors into the home quarters from line out at quarter flag. Drummond obtained possession, and put in a capital run. Widnes were awarded a free kick,Rigg relieving pressure by making his mark in goal line. Clarke pot in some good work, and again placed the homesters on the aggres•;ive. Greenwood made a capi- tal run, and Rochdale almost scored a goal, from a penalty. Dick Brennan put an end to a grand run by Hill just in time, Wright sending the ball to midfield, but directly afterwards Sharrocks tested Brennan's defensive powers, the result being a scrimmage in the opposite posts. The home forwards transferred play by a grand passing movement. Wright was pulled up on the line by Rigg, and Clarke missed a good opportunity, but a moment later he made amends by scoring at the corner flag. Alford failed at a difficult place. The game continued to he very fast, each team attacking in turn, but without any tangible result. After the Wid. nes lines had a very narrow escape, Rigg was called upon, and defended finely. Half time—Widnes 1 try, St.Clinnent's nil. Final result :—Widnes 2 tries, 1 minor, St. Clement's 1 goal..

div.p: RUNCORN V. OLD EDVIARDIANS.

Runcorn were badly fixed behind; men having to change places. The Edwardians had a good team upi Riley started at 3.20, Moore making a capital returnrAhrains returning finely to Fox, who put In touch. The play centred tor a time, uplift Fox got away and seAred„ Adams making a good btd for goal. On the resumption the home side played very tame, and the Edwardians by rushes kept the Cheshire men well in check. Ifiulkner got well away, but Fox inter- cepted and the chance to Crompton was lost. For a con- sidoreble period the Ididlaaders were kept in their half. Runcorn experiencing very hard lines. Frequent free kicks tell to Runcorn„ awing to, the off-side play ef the visitors. An exciting piece of play now took place. Houghton picked up, in his own, quarter, and racing away dodged through the whole of the Rd wavdians ana scored close to the poets amid much excitement, the goal kick failing. Nicol re-started„ and Crompton got off and looked like /scoring, but passing, lost the chance. Fox next made a clever run along touch, which Houghton checkmated. Runcorn were now on the Nod wardians' line,.but could not score.. Abrams now went half-back and another forward was put out of the pack, still the Old Boys played a, very strong defence. Final result.—Runcorn 2 goals„L try, I.minor, Edward- inns, 1 try.

div.head: BLICKRURN MURDER,
div.p: THE BLICKRURN MURDER,

Some excitement was caused in. Blackbure on Tuesday by the discovery that Cross Duckworth, now under re- mand on suspicion of having committed the Blackburn murder, had secreted in bis coat pocket a rope with a running noose, evidently with ttse intention of com- mitting suicide. The inquest on Mite Barnes,. the child who was mur- dered at Witton„ Blackburn, on. the Bth inst.. was con- tinned at Blackburn on Thursday, and again adjourned. Cross Duckworth,, who lain custody in connection with the murder, was present.. Among the witnesses was Harry Riding,. aged ten, who stated thrt at about the time when the crime must have been committed he saw a man running towards Witton Park gate with a child in his ar ms,, and he believed that the man he saw With Duckworth. He picked him out from among several , other men at the police-station. Other witnesses were called who expressed their belief that the prisoner was the man seen by them loitering in the neighbour- hood of Witton Park gate shortly before the child's body was found. Dr. Wheatley, of Blackburn, who made the post-mortem examination, stated that death was caused by suffocation, arising from a handkerchief having been crammed into the girl's mouth so tightly that she could not breathe. All ARREST AT FRODSHAM.

A considerable amount of excitement prevailed in Frodsham on Wednesday, on its becoming known that the police had arrested a man on suspicion of being con- cerned in the Blackburn murder. On Thursday morn- ing the man, named Peter Welch, was brought before, Mr. A. Thomas,at the Police Court, when the circura- stances leading to his arrest were fully strged by P.S. Doyle. Be said that seeing the description, of the man, in the "'Police Gazette" required for the Blackburn murder, he visited the lodging house is. ship-street, Frodsbam. on Tuesday night, and saw Welch, and thinking he corresponded therewith, he ques- tioned him, but he got very evasive answers, and witness told him they should detain hina until samething was heard from Blackburn Be had communicated with Superintendent Myers, of Blackburn, who had tele- graphed " Welch is not the man wanted." Witness was sorry on behalf of the police that Welch had been de- tained so long, but this was entirely due to tho evasive answers he gave to the questions put to him. He asked now that the man be discharged. Mr. Thomas, in dis- charging him, said it was always best to give straight- forward answers to any queetioas put to bun.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

For two weeks there was no football at Wilderspoo and the change in the aspect of the Causeway during that fortnight was noticeably great and impressive to the pedestrian. To one accustomed to travelling that thoroughfare on Saturday afternoons they were two weeks of inexplicable peacefulness and tranquility ; a mixture/ of intense and blessed quietude coupled with an unmolested opportunity to keep one's boots clean, and travel along the footpath without luffing and backing water liken broken-winded tugboat. It was just lus- cious! No, "madding crowd" of enthusiastic foot- ballers with eager looks and stout boots hustled you about like & witness in a police court. No heavy roll of tramping feet squashed down your tender sprouting corn. No, the corn continued to sprout, and the oaly other claimant to the road was the low wailing windr which didn't blow the russet autumn leaves aroued, but just howled liken moonstruck puppy and sneaked up. the bottom of your pants.

And so to a mani whose unfortunate self-consciauenest and large understanding won't allow hito to use any- thing but the whole footpath, Saturday was rife with bitter disappointment. The Warrington footballera. were playing Mossley,, and they had issued a placard to the effect that "This., match will positively fair place." And it did. One plkyer got bis arm dislocated,, another iot his head broken,. and the hopeful pedestrian re- signedly remodelled himself into an improvised foot- cleaner and recoiled unobtrusively into the gutter I A spectator engrosses in the match, and watching an ex- ' caking feature of the game with avidity, mistakenly sliced off the end of his, ;lager instead of a quid of to- bacco. Another enthusiaet triumphantly brought his hand with a gesture of approbation down upon a stvmp with a spike in it. All thiaia evidence to show that be- yond doubt the match i did take place.

But as a football performance the match was even a greater success than as ameniercise for amateur St.John'a Ambulance men ! Both teams seemed to be equally bent upon winning, and for Cher first. part of the game both played with a strength and energy uncommon even+ at Wilderspool. Indeed, had•it not been for Boscow, the• indomitable back, Warrington's chances would have been, like the atmosphere last week, rather hazy. A dozen times the Mossley men would have got , through, had it not been for the home custo- dian's sharp and sure interference. He gave emphasis on Saturday to his real fitness,for a corner in the county team. While he kept the onslaught of the enemy in check, the home men by constant application to their opponents, brough, them down to, a stage of weariness, so that when the second half came Warrington began to show signs of victory and Plumpton and Tolley scored a try each, botk within a few moments.

Plumpton was in splendid form, and was always up to the front in a manner which won him many lusty shouts of " Well done Plumpton." Plumpton really deserves praise, for his alertnewand smartness are very noticeable. As three-quarters Bate and Evans did a little better than a few weeks ago. Amongst the for- words Fair Turner, the Tall Athlete,Ashton, and Nevins, were all conspicuously alert. The combined working of the forwards, as a body, WAS rattier Toone, and each man was inclined to show a little toorauda individualism. It WAS at the close of the game that the play became exciting, and for at least 15 minutes there WAS one con- tinual chorus of vociferous criticism on the game. The play indeed became fast and furious- then, and passing of a smart character WAS common. Smack Bate was taking a prominent pact in this, when he met with an accident which terminated the gamer.

When within • few yards of the visitors' posts, " Smack " made a sudden dash for the ball ; somehow he lost his footing and fell. He rolled over heavily and shouted. It 1110 seen that he was-ir*red, and play was suspended. Examination showed that unfortunate Bate had broken his arm and his colinr bone again. He was removed (rem the field and play was resumed. Before the game had been going two, minutes there was another howl. The next moment Donohue staggered and fell, with a gash an inch long,bn his forehead. It was just five minutes from timet, bat the game was brought to a close.

To Smack Bate the accident is a very serious one, for the injury is on the same spot where he was severely Injured a few weeks ago. It looks very black for his okances in the ranks of the County team. --- What next P Oh, " yes " ; the cup. competition. Well, don't crowd round too much, the-Virarrington team has sot yet placed its delicate haad of snowy white flesh upoa the" tin tankard," known soma:irnes as the silver cup. It hasn't quite got to the top of the list yet, but It. the fault of that confounded smallpox, or the German measles, or whatever it is. These axe the results up to Saturday

LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY. LECTURE ON SOCRATES.

On-Monday evening a lecture was delivered fl the Museum Lecture Room, under the auspices of the Warrington Literary and Philosopuical Society by the Rev. D L Bedford, 8.A., on Socrates. Mr. R. Davies,. president of the society presided. There was a large attendance. The Chairman, prefaced the lecture with some observations, in the conrse- of which he expressed his regret that in coneeq,uesice of the prevalence of small- pox the lecture by Mr. Barry Furniss was not to take place. He also made some very feeling andaulogistie references to Mr. John Walker, late proprietor- and editor of this joui nal, which appear la our obituary article upon Csat gentlem .n. The lecturer said of Socrates that his leading idea was briefly thia• that all virtue was knowledge. This was the principle on which he attempted to reform humanity. He left cis with the impression drat he regar led the good as identi- cal with the,-useful„ in other words that he considered advantagerand disadvantage the standard of good aril evil, and that man should live virtuously because virtue carried withdt the-greatest rewards both from God and man. Plato on the. other hand held that Socrates be- lieved virtue-to be good in itself ap.irt from itsconee- quences, and reno charged him with inconsistency in his teachings-on the subject. Socrates ignored the human will in his defttaitioni of virtue. St. Paul,the Christian pint- : osopher, wasmucii truer to fact when he said' When would do good,.evik is present with me." The Socratic theory exalted the head at the expense of the heart. , Radford denied-that S.crates's system of exacting tions as a proof of knowledge was always a test of thls,aa- serting that a man was riot necessarily to be called ignorant 11 because lie cculd not give a defioicion of his ichms,.sioes : much of ourrknowledge was implicit.—The Chairrn.an opened the discussion at theclose, and Mr. Gibson Smith who proposed a 'Soto. of thanks to the lecturer, followed, Councillor Moults, seconded, and Messrs. Jolley, Peera, and White supported it, and made observations on the lecture. The-vote waa heartily carried, and the lecturer's acknowledgment closed the proceedings.

FARNEERS CON FE RE NCE AT WARRIIiGTON. TIM "'THREE r 8 " DEMANDED. A conference of farmers and others Interested is agriculture was held on Wednesday night, at the Farmers'-Stores,.Warrington. div.head: TIT-BITS. HE FABLE OF THE WOLF, THE FOX, AND THE ASS.
div.p: TIT-BITS. HE FABLE OF THE WOLF, THE FOX, AND THE ASS.

The Lion, as king of the beasts, made a law, that no teaat should, without lawful cause, do any hurt to another, and should come once a-year to court, to confess, and be absolved or punished, according to his deserts. Now it happened that the Wolf and the Fox were going thither together, and over- taking the As, on the road, said to him, "Brother, It is a long way to court, and it certainly must be much more tedious to you than to ourselves, lee of your slow pace; but we can save the t3rcle of going thither, if you think fit. Let us three coulees ourselves to one another, and send our absolutions to court, attested by two of us as Witnesses."

The Ass liked the proposal ; into a clover field they went, and the Fox thus confessed himself first.:—"lt happened, as I was going one night through a village, a Cock, by his loud crowing, dis- turbed all the people that were asleep; at which I grew very angry, and bit off his head; then fear- mg that the stench of his dead body might be offensive to the Hens, I ate him up. Nevertheless it happened, three days after, as I was going by the same village, those very Hens spied me; and, instead of thanking me for the great kindness I had done them, cried out, ' Murderer, murderer Then I, in defence of my honour, killed three of them • and, lest they should have stunk and offended the' neighbourhood; ate them up too. This is all I have done; for which I now await your, sentence." The Wolf thereupon expressed himself thus "You have indeed offended against the letter of our monarch's law, but not against the meaning of it; since your intentions were honourable, to take care of the quiet of men, and to vindicate your injured reputation : If, therefore, you will promise never to be so hasty again in killing any beast, I vote for your absolution." This the Fox readily did; and the Ass joined in opinion with the Wolf, who then thus began his conleasion "As I was one day walking along, I saw a Sow trampling down the corn of a poor peasant, and tearing it up by the roots, while her hungry Pigs were strayed far from her, and could not get them- selves out of the mire; so that I, growing very angry at the great mischief she did the peasant, and at her neglect of motherly duty, killed and ati her up. Three days after, chancing to go again the same way, I observed that those Pigs were grown very lean; and reflecting that, through want of their mother's milk, they would certainly die a languishing death, I put an end to thekt miseries, and ate them up too. This is all I hail to confess."

The Fox instantly argued in this manner "Though you confess to have killed both motet and children, and though it seems at first sight that you have heinously offended against the law of out king, yet I see, nevertheless, that your intentions were good; to prevent mischief from falling upon men, to stir up a mother to her duty, and to show compassion to her miserable children, are virtues that no law can forbid or punish. I therefore declare you absolved." To which the Ass agreed. The Ass then made his confession :—" You both know," said he, "that it is not in my nature to de hurt to other beasts, nor to shed blood; and, therefore, you cannot expect to hear any such thing from me; but, to content you, I will relate to you what happened innocently to me, while I was in the service of a master. He was an old man, and apt to take cold in his feet; so that, when he travelled, to keep them dry and warm, he was wont to stick a little hay in his shoes. Now I carried him, one winter, to an ind; whtp he was to lie all night; add when we came to thaa-iclhe innkeeper br_ought.MT,lrair of thy. frdippers, that -bis dift7l-I:hoes 'Might not soil the house; so Oat he pulled them off, and left them without, and me by them. In short, my master and his host found them. selves so well in the chimney-corner, that they never thought of poor me, but left me all night in the bittea cold, without giving me a handful of for4l so that I ate up all the hay that stuck in his aloes. This Is all I have to say; if you will call i a con- fession, you may : however, I think nothing can be said against it." "Oh I" said the Fox, immediately, "this is not indeed an offence against the letter of the law, which mentions only the doing hurt to beasts, and takes no notice of eating of hay; but if we reflect on the dangerous oonsequences of this action, and that Bo reverend a creature as a chill, aged man, by being thus robbed cf his hay in the winter, an the next day continuing his road without it, might have caught a cold, a cough, and a colic, that would have brought his grey hairs to the grave; whoever, I say, reflects on this, cannot but be of my opinion—which is, that the Ass largely deserves to die. Cousin Wolf, what say you to this matter?" "I," said the Wolf, "am of opinion, that, by reason of the ill consequences that might have attended this action, the Ass deserves a double death, and to be made an example to others." With that he leaped upon him, and tore out his throat, and the Fox and he immediately ate him Irl3.

To some one or other, And I think to my brother, Because I foresaw, That my brethren-in-law, It I did not oar*, Would come in for their share, Which I nowise intended, TM their manners are mended. And of that, God knows, there's no Wig I do therefore enjoin, And do strictly command, Of which, witness my hand, That nought I have got Be brought into hotch-pot But I give and devise, As much as in me lies, To the son of my mother, My own dear brother, To have and to hold. A TRIFLING EXCEPTION.

In 1643, St Preuil, the governor of Amiens wise depended much on a stratagem that he had con- ceived for seizing upon Arras, was anxious to engage a soldier named Courcelles to execute it. "I have made choioe of you," said he to him one day, "as the most prudent soldier that I know, for a blow that will make your fortune. The business is to surprise Arnie; and hear how I have planned it. You shall disguise yourself as a peasant, and go and sell fruit in the place. After you have done tills some time, you must quarrel with some person, and kill him with a poniard. You must suffer yourself to be taken, you wi'l be tried on the spot, and be condemned to be hanged. You know the custom of Arras is to have their executions out of the city. It is on this circum- stance that my design depends. I will place an ambuscado near the gate by which you shall be brought out. My people will render themselves meters of those who shall come out who belong to the spectacle. I will march in the instant to their assistance, and make myself master of the dace; which as soon as I am, I shall rescue you. I his is my project; what do you say to it, ?" "It is tine," replied (3ourociles, " but the thing deserves con- sideration." "It does," said St. Preuil ; "think of it, and to•nrirrow let me have your resolution." The next day Courcelles waited on his commander. " Well, my brave fellow," said St. Preuil, " what do you think of my project now?' "Sir," replied Courcelles, "it is admirable ; only I should like that you would give rue the command of the ambus- cade, and take your,elf the haAet of fruit."

A LADY having begged Prince Maurice to tell her Who ,was the first captain of the age, he excused himself from exp-essing his opinion on a matter so delicate; modesty not permitting him to name him- self,and his sense of merit preventing him from rieldUg to another a glory which belonged to him- Self. At last, being pressed, he replied, "Madam, Vie Marquis de Boinola is the second."
