PROPOSED BRIDGE FOR RUNCORN.

Sir,—From your paper of Saturday it appears the Runcorn Commissioners contemplate borrowing £30,000 to wards the cost, £lBO,OOO, for making a vehicular bridge to cross the Mersey. As a property owner, I enter my protest against such a wild scheme, and one which will never pay the interest of even 4 per cent. on the sum advanced by Runcorn alone. Besides, there is the fact of other large undertakings being almost I always nnder-estimated, viz., the Ship Canal, Mersey Tunnel, and Vynrwy water scheme. It is more likely to cost £280,000, so that Runcorn would again be called upon to contribute. The promoters of the scheme should try to float it as a "limited." They would soon be on I their beam ends. Why not call public meetings on such an important outlay, and then have a poll of the whole body of ratepayers throughout Cheshire ? Many people are interested in such schemes who do not care a straw for public money. What interest does the hydraulic. lift st Anderton pay ?—Yours, ROBERT FOULKES. November 14th, 1892.

VIVISECTION AND THE MEDICAL MORALITY. Sir,—l would fain believe that your report of the lecture delivered by a Dr. Mouncey on vivisection was either incomplete or inaccurate. In this discourse we have frequent reference to the benefits derived by the medical profession and the public from the practice in question. Now, as to the medicos, it is of use to them— in puts money into their pockets, and, like the present lecture, is a mild form of advertisement. In this way it takes the place ef the more direct, if less professional, query, "Have you a bad leg ?" Surely your report should have stated that among the diagrams and charts which rendered the subject so lucid, there was one showing a vivisector's torture table, and the number of helpless victims annually sacrificed to this medical Moloch. A few details as to the means by which all the " benefits " are obtained, would have been highly interesting to the audience ; and if, to this, could have been added a few practical experiments upon members of that audience, such as taking out a kidney, pricking the spinal marrow, producing peritonitis, stabbing the eye and introducing therein inflammatory filth, the real facts would have been brought home to them. Time, however, did not permit of the due prolongation of these experimental agonies. I say no word as to the morality of this ethically indefensible practice of animal inquisition. As what is morally wrong cannot be prac- tically right, I hold that animals ought to be protected from the perpetration of this wrong upon them. I challenge any pro-vivisectionist to show to the contrary. 'At this lecture, as elsewhere, when possible, the seamy side' of this question was discreetly kept out of sight, and the audience went home innocently unconscious of the dread secrets of the vivisector's table. Had this lecturer not been a special pleader, he might have withdrawn the thin veil separating his auditory from the ghastly horrors of this great unrighteousness.—Yours, &c., JOHN PEERS.

Penketh, November 14th, 1892, P.S.—Since the above left my hands I have read the Horsley-Ruffer attempt to bolster up the practice of vivisection on utilitarian grounds. Stripped )f the fogs of verbiage, the central argument stands thus :—The results of vivisection are useful to mankind and animals. What can be shown to be useful to man and animals must be morally justifiable. So say these special pleaders for scientific cruelty—whatever is useful to man is right Using this as a corollary; let me show a practical appli- cation of the argument. I. Warrington is suffering from smallpox. 11. The total destruction of the disease by stamping out—would be highly beneficial to our people. This may be speedily and completely accomplished by killing and cremating all infected persons. 111 Hence this stamping out is quite justifiable morally' The fact that this would involve the practice of murder is of course a mere incidental detail, and need not deter anyone from its adoption who can swallow the ordinary vivisector's morality ! jji

A CAP AND A CORNER FOR "A LEARNER." Sir,—l see my dipterous friend is still on the nave, and in imagination,—still raising the dust. Surely, the old fabulist must have known our only Fly in some previous stage of existence—for he hits him off exactly —the type of conceited insignificance. It is a sight to make the angels weep—with laughter—to see a natur- ally dull man attempting to be funny ! He handles a joke as a bear does a musket, and his gambols resemble nothing so much as a cow in a cage. Now our" Learner" never was intended by nature to be funny, but, to be the source of fun for others. In this respect he is a mine —not a very deep one perhaps—but still a mine of out- cropping absurdities very valuable these dull times. Yes ! I have been tickled by this insect who rides on another's chariot and claims to have made the dust ! Paroxysms I have had in perusing him—.lccompanied by an outbreak of broad-grins. I find some of the pro- fessedly comic papers much less laughter-provoking than the strained funniosities and the comical misap- prehensions of this prototype of ifiop's Fly. And then there is the fun of holding our little friend up be- fore an admiring public as an object lesson; as an ex- ample of bad grammar and worse logic, tempered by very indifferent science. He is quite a study, our " Learner !" I call him ours. I have made him mine. May his shadow never be less, or his dullness greater ! Be talks of my " armoury of invective 1" The man who has to borrow an opprobious appellative from a congenial spirit and who, with the pertinacity of exceed- ing dullness, parades it as his only credential to be a wit, cannot claim to be the possessor of an" armoury of invective " but makes up for this deficiency by mak- ing a noise with his one rusty blunderbuss. The narrow limits of our printed correspondence are much too con- stricted for " A Learner "to find that scope for his absurdities which his genius demands, so he goes " Down by the sea " and, as usual, gets adrift. It is quite characteristic of the man to find him taking au grand seriaux what was so evidently intended as a joke! But a joke has evidently no affinity with the cerebrum of " A Learner." Not only can he not assimilate a joke, but he is also a fearful example that a person, can have some rules of logic off by rote, and yet not be able to reason. When I have leisure I will again dip into Watt, Mill, and Whately to find the logic of the assertion that because the savage kills off the useless and effete mem- bers of his family, therefore " the cultured man of the 19th century is excluded from the study of nature!" if this laughter-provoking person is amusing when posing as a logician, equally so is he when striking an attitude as a Natural Philosopher. Barring the philoso- pher the title is descriptively perfect. How very natural for instance, is he in this sentence—" The conclusion he comes to must not conflict with the great law of the con- servation of energy." ! ! ! This completely " flab- bergasts" me ! 'f.his profound truth is comparable only in its inconsequential intangibility with an arithmetical problem worked at for months, by another Warrington worthy. He was " just on the point of solving it," when someone told him that something more than the " binomial theorem "would be required to get the cap- tain's name from the given dimensions of the ship ! Perhaps in his next he will kindly tell us how the " great law " of gravitation affects the conclusion of Biologists ? Also whether the law that 2 x 2 equals 4 mili- tates against the undoubted fact that "A Learner "had a tail in a pre-natal stage of his existence ? I am asked as a reductio ad absurdum what I should do to a fruit-stealing urchin intruding in my garden. As a reasoning being I should, in the first instance, reason with him, and, if he really and not merely nominally was " A Learner " he would take warning and never again intrude upon, Yours truly, JOHN PEERS. ?.S.—With other than reasoning beings, literary or other, I have equally effective methods.
PETTY LANDLORDS IN NEWTON-LE-

advance of wages, and the Opportunity is seined to demand a general advance, of rent; It is rumoured that a rate on a small scale will probably be made, to pay for ' the new Town Hall, and a mass of correspondence in the local press is instigated, the object being to pave the way for another increase of rent. Now,the proposed increase of the water rate, is quickly pounced upon, as a pretext ' for still further fleecing the unfortunate tenant. Now, sir, the landlord already derives a large profit from this I rate, in the following manner. For the supply of water to a cottage a charge is made of is. 6d. per quarter ; the tenant is charged in his rent 3d. per week to meet this rate. The increased charge will be 2s. 2d. per quarter, or 83. Bd. per annum. The tenant's rent is in- creased another 3d. per week, and by this means the landlord secures 20s. a year for what he pays but Bs. Bd., truly a gigantic interest. But there are landlords and landlords, and I should be indeed sorry to cast the odium of these sharp practices on innocent shoulders. I The action of those landlords I have referred to is al Istriking contrast to that of property owners of some social status, who have not increased their rents for forty years. Now, let me endeavour to point out the cause of this state of affairs. Some years ago the local building society was inaugurated, most of its supporters fondly hoping in years to come to be their own landlords. What is the result ? The only people to whom any bene- fits have accrued are a select “nv of the clique of petty landlords, who snapped up all the old property which came into the market, and by degrees have increased the rents over 50 per cent. A grocer's shop in High-st., Prior to its purchase by one of these landlords, was rented for 4s. per week; it is now Bs. On the other side of the street, property which was rented for gii a year has been raised to £2O. Some cottages in one street not long ago were 3s. 9d. a week, and this in- cluded a piece of land used as a garden. The present landlord considered that the value of the property would ne enhanced if the garden were taken away ; accordingly, he appropriated the land, and, as an equi- valent, increased the rent is. a week. In another street tenants have paid £l5 a year for fourteen years and uowards(£2lo) for houses that never cost £l2O. Surely they might reasonably expect to escape this iniquitous increase. But no ; the landlord is on the march, and, he will have his pound of flesh. Again, two blocks of pro- perty, I have in my mind, formerly rented at 2s. 3d. and 48. 3d., are now 4s. 3d. and ss. 3d. respectively. There is only one conclusion—an obvious one—to be dr..wn from these facts, and that is, that instead of being a blessing to the inhabitants of Newton, the building society, whilst being an unquestionable benefit to a few, has been a curse to the general body of householders.

The remedy? Well, sir, if the monopoly enjoyed by this band of landlords could be destroyed, I think the remedy would be a natural consequence. I would res- pectfully throw out the suggestion that if cne of our large employers of labour would only protect his employes against the rapacity of these land sharks, he would earn the gratitude of the inhabitants at large. If he could be induced to erect a number of good cot- tages,and allow some of his most trustworthy employee tis purchase them on the co-operative principle, I think he would secure a good percentage on the capital invested, and, by striking at the monopoly,relieve the oppression, and prove himself *nee more a benefactor to the COM. munity.—Yours, Azc.,
A VICTIM.

div.head: VACCINATION SCARE.
div.p: THE VACCINATION SCARE.

Sir,—Has it ever occurred to you that the present epidemic of smallpox,may be due to the weather? Per- haps you smile at the idea, but I will explain. The past few summers have been very cold, and our towns- people when they have taken their annual day's outing at the seaside have not been tempted to enter the water for their annual wash down. The consequence has been that their systems have become clogged with effete matter, and they have become fit subjects for any dis- ease that may visit us. Of course, you will pooh-pooh this by saying that we have baths in town. Ah, but have we? Have we a bath fit for any townsman to enter ? For myself, I should as soon think of bathing in Sankey Brook, as of entering the Legh-at. establish- ment. But then we have our new baths ? Yes, and while the foundations are setting, our people have to go unwashed. There can be no doubt that the Corporation are to lame for the present state of things by not pTo- viding proper bathing accommodation for the inhabit- ants. A well-known medical writer says smallpox owes its virulence to uncleanly habits, and (Oh ! horrors 0 the eating of flesh! div.head: EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE EPIDEMIC.

Sir.—Will you kindly find space in your columns for the following. lam informed that the Medical Officer and all the staff are using a certain kind of disinfectant for the prevention of small-pox, which I consider ought to be made as public as Possible, as the disease is spread- ing with alarming rapidity. No one can tell when or where he or she may contract the disease. I consider that if there is a preventative, the thing cannot be too widely known. I should like to see something from an official of the town to say what disinfectant is the best. —Yours truly, 105, Manchester-rd., Warrington.
ROBERT SHAW.
A SUGGESTION.

Sir,—Being desirous that everything should be done that will in any way tend to stamp out the present loathsome disease, I would very respectfully suggest to the Health Committee, and their medical officer, the advisability of at once considering as to,and,if necessary, ordering the day and Sunday schools to be closed say for the remainder of the year. I am much surprised that this has not been done before. In previous epide- mics of a less alarming nature than the present one,this order has been given. If it is found advisable to close the Free Library, and Reading room, and to call in all books, there is in my opinion a greater reason why schools should be closed.—Yours truly, P. E. Winwick-road, 18th Nov. 1892. ' d t DOCTORS AND MINISTERS. Sir,—The doctors tell us that the present epidemic is infectious, and also ccntageous. Now, if this be so, how is it that neither doctors, nor nurses, nor officials, who are in constant attendance at the h not taken this contagious disease? Have' what disinfectants do they use, in ordei selves from contagion. It is the duty of the public Medical Officer of Health, to make known the disinfec- tant, which they use with such beneficial results to themselves, so that the people may know what to use to check the disease, and thus to stamp it out. Where are our ministers • the other day a woman died in the the hospital, and for an hour before she died she asked for a minister, or clergyman, to be brought to pray with her ! Have any of our ministers, of any creed or sect, been to visit the sick and afflicted in the hospital. If not, it reflects no credit upon the ministerial fraternity of our town, that they have neglected this duty ; and left the people to die without a hope to cheer their lying hour.—Yours truly, U. div.head: HOW TO STOP THE SMALLPDX.
div.p: HOW TO STOP THE SMALLPDX.

Sir,—Now that our" City Fathers" have successfully established a hospital, which has proved a centre of infection in our midst, and gracefully retired, it is quite time that the residents took the matter in their own hands. That the smallpox can be practically stamped out in about three weeks is certain from ex- perience in other places, and the only remedy required is re-vaccination. In Sheffield, during the years 1887-8 56,233 persons were re-vac3inated. Of these two were doubtfully attacked, and none died. In the London smallpox hospitals, out of 10,403 cases, there were no deaths where the vaccination had been performed within five years, and two only where it had been performed within ten years, previous to the attack. . . . .

In that p-estilenlial city, Hmaburg, re-vaccination has been compulsory since 1874. From 1870 to 1873 the average deaths from smallpox in Hamburg were 3in every 100 ; after 1874 they were reduced to 1 in every 5,000, although the city is specially open to infection from all parts of the world. The smallpox death rate of London averages twenty times this. He-vaccination was made compulsory throughout Prussia in 1875. For the five years before this, the average death rate from smallpox was 11 per 1,000 ; for the five years after it was less than 1 per 1,000, and this rate remains con- stant as an average with little variation. The fear of transmission of other diseases need have no existence, as pure vaccine lymph is obtained direct from healthy calves. There is no doubt, whatever, from the reports carefully examined, from all the civilised countries in the world, that re-vaccination affords absolute protection for five years, and almost perfect protection for five years more. Rs-vaccination has no doubt been recommended by our local authorities, but their action, or inaction, has been such that very little confidence appears to be shown in their unsupported opinions. The above figures have been taken from the reports of governments, whose interest it is to put an end to dangerous contagion. If all employers of labour would first set the example them- selves and refuse to employ any persons who have not been re-vaccinated, or whose families have not been :e-vaccinated, the epidemic would at once die out for want of subjects to keep it alive. If this is not done nrobably the town will be as plague-stricken as Ham- burg has recently been, meaning ruin and starvation to hundreds if not thousands. There can be no question as to the figures I give, which are taken from the offi- cial reports of cases Austria, Prussia, Berlin, Ham- burg, London, Paris, and Vienna. There can be no question as to the results, which, although they vary in each year's reports, point to vaccination as the only immediate and absolute remedy for the trouble which is in our midst and which is still rapidly increasing.— Yours Sze., THOMAS FLETCHER. November 15th, 1895.

AN EIGHT HOURS WORK DAY. Sir,—The " Examiner "has done well in opening its columns for the discussion of the Eight Hour Question. Although it is only a phase of the social revolt, it is the most prominent of all the burning labor questions now standing on the social agenda for settlement. I always read with pleasure the ;letters of " Cymro." Be brings a sort of hard-headed experience to bear up- on the questions he deals with, that helps us along ; but lam afraid that, upon this one q uestion, he has nar- rowed his usually broad vision down to a too narrow scale. Why should he make, repeat, or perpetuate that rather stale charge against labour leaders,thal "they tell their hearers, what they like to hear, rather than en- deavour to teach them what is practical." He knows, as well as anyone, that the labour leaders of to-day. especially those of England are remarkable for nothing more than their strong individualist tendencies. To my mind, the strongest, and purest leader of the workers, who has risen in this 19th century and who has, to our great sorrow, passed over, Mr. Bradlaugh, never con- sidered what his hearers eked or disliked, but spoke out with a manly voice the results of a profound study of sociology. Like Mr. Wilson, the Durham labour leader, he was opposed to legislation upon the question at issue, and told his hearers so. Can " Cymro " put his finger on one, amongst the leaders, who deserves the harsh I ;terms he uses? I think not. The fierce light of public ' inpinion, would soon prove too much for the demagogue, so as a matter of fact, his occupation is gone. I make bold to say, the questions " Cymro "puts to his readers, October 15th, are not at all to the point, and the question, when decided will not be settled upon out economic theory. It is, therefore, desirable we should clear the ground a little and know . v where we stand, and I ask as bluntly as possi- ble :is the work we are doing necessary ? If not neces- sary shall it be cleared out? If cleared out, what shall we find for the added number to the out of work ranks to do, if ten hours is to remain the minimum for a day's, labour? Regardless of the taunt of" Utopian " being thrown at me, I must declare, as others have done before me, and as others must believe possible, or they would cease their ameliorative work, this life can be made worth liv- ing. Is it desirable that such Infernos as Krupp's of Germany. or Armstrong of Northumberland, should,year by year, put before the public such prosperous business leports as those recently issued ? Is it in the interests of useful work, and civilization, that the Government naval yards of Great Britain, Germany.Russia,America, and Italy, should crowd the oceans with the death deal- ing hells, such as the iron-clads are? If anyone answers in the affirmative, why, then, let all the religious and moral influences how at work, cease, for it can only be PO much humbug. "In order that tobacco, wine, hasnish, opium, may be produced in sufficient quanti- tie, to keep pace with the present enormous rate of con- sumption, millions and millions of acres of the best soil, among populations sorely in need of land, are set apart 'for the cultivation of rye, potatoes, hemp, poppy,vines, and tobacco, and millions of human beings—in England one-eighth of the entire population—devote all their lives to the manufacture of these stupifying stimulants." don't know what the future may have in store fot us in the way of fresh trade developments, but, if only the ew trades (?) I have indicated are done away with, along with the standing armies, some new channels will have to'be found to find ten hours work per day for the extra labour thus thrown into the market. I allow the above is not quite within the realm of practi- cal politics, but it may suggest thoughts for young minds. Since 1832 we have made great mistakes. Watt. Arkwright, and Crompton should have been smothered at their birth. Steam should have been confined to the kettle, and then we shouldn't have been troubled with the fiery horses on sea and land. Better still, we ought never to have had the franchise, or the education bill passed. What happy, piggish times we should now be having. But the "Masters" are now educated, and they say distinctly that they will have more leisure, and no one must ask, "for what " ? Shall we get it? Yes, study Mr. Chamberlain's "unauthorized programme" as laid before the Liberal Union party, Oct. 29th. This, it io sure, is the plank that will ultimately grow into a platform to be put forth as a bid for the workmen's vote by a man who intends to be Premier before long. Look at London at this moment. Hundreds assembling daily on Tower Hill demanding food-id work, and parading the east end, always under the red and black flag. Think of the strike now pending in L.aeashire with near 100,00 g men out. A good deal of this is laid at the door of over-praduction—labour saving machinery resulting in over-production, and thousands naked and hungry. To me it seems as if, not ten hours, nor yet eight hours was required, but that we should give over mak- ing plush to clothe the flunkeys, and oleo-margarine to feed the hungry. Of course the admirers of the old political economists wail about competition, demanding that the animate, and inanimate plant now at the bidding of capital, shall be left unfettered to work out its sweet will, but the argument is played out. In Australia, where they have worked eight hours, the agitation is now for seven. In the States, the agitation is intense, but there, as in England, plutocracy is only hastening on its owa end. Yes, the " Masters "are educated, or nearly so. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: LOOKING FCR NEW ACCOMWDATION.
div.p: LOOKING FCR NEW ACCOMWDATION.

The sub-committee appointed by the Health Commit- tee to obtain a site for another hospita3. have not yet been successful in their elforts. One of the stipulations In that they shall not select a site within a! mile of any dwelling. Dr. Thompson,. the Local Government Com- =Winner, gave this instruction, and the sub-committee are finding great difficulty in carrying it out. Several sites have been proposed, tint none have been suitable. The report that the selected site was on Pear Tree Farm, Houghton, is not correct. This lack of accommodation is assuming a serious aspect, as the dailyuincreasing cases cannot be isolated, and have to be treated at the patients' homes. The infected houses are identified by a printed notice affixed on the doors. BUSINESS AT A DEAD LOCK.

THE CAUSE. We have been informed by several leading tradesmen that their weekly takings are falling off in a manner in which threatens to bring their business to a complete dead lock in a few days. These are tradesmen who• supply country people. One Sankey-st, grocer has,ex- perienced a loss of £4O per week during the past fort- night,. and says that when his representatives visit country customers they are peremptorily dismissed. Another tradesmen—possibly the largest grocer in, the town—tells us a similar tale. Much of this is no doubt in consequence of the epidemic being conveyed from, Warrington to several places in Cheshire,and the issuing of a circular by Dr. Fox, medical officer for that county,, to the effect that people should avoid any contact with anything or anybody from Warrington.

div.head: SX VACCINATION STATIONS.
div.p: SX VACCINATION STATIONS.

The Warrington Corporation are providing six. vaccination stations for grattnous vaccination In different parts of the town, which will be open every evening from 7 till 10, commencing on Monday next. A medical gentleman will be appointed to each station.

THE MEDICAL PROFESSIONS OPINION. At a meeting of the medical profession held on Wed— nesday at the Town Hall, Dr. C. N. Spinks presiding, it was decided "That it is the unanimous opinion of this meeting that vaccination and re-vaccination remain the best possible methods of stamping out the present epidemic." REFERENCE AT THE POLICE COURT.

At the Borough Magistrates' Court, on Monday, Alder— man Harrison said before they commenced business he desired in the most respettfnl and defereatial manner to suggest the propriety of their not hailtig the coprtl crowded any more than they could possibly helo, during. the present epidemic. He was glad that on his right sat Dr.Gornallaud that Di.Spinks was present,and they' would both:satisty them as to whether it would not be desirable in the interests of the public that that course-1 should be pursued. They were endeavouring as mush as possible to event 'the undue congregation of larger number or people than was absolutely necessary. He was afraid that in the Borough Court, on Monday, particularlyithere'were a number of persons who simply came to gratify curiosity ; and by crowding together unnecessarily they might possibly ba helping to spread the disease which-it was such a great calamity to have prevalent in the town ; and which he hoped and trusted the d;;ease would soon be extinguished. Dr. Gomel': had just whispered to him that it would have been de- sirable for him to suggest the propriety of everytiody being vaccinated'. He was sure if everybody would consent to be vaccinated, they might by making a little personal sacrifice for the, time, ultimately do great good to the public.
OUTBREAK AT NEWTON.

On Wednesday Dr. Watkins, medical officer of health, received notification from Dr. Paterson, that a man named Daniel Hy lance, living in Crow-lane, Newton, was suffering from an attack of smallpox. Steps were immediately taken to isolate the case, and the same day the patient was removed to the Hope Hospital, Warring- ton. OUTBREAK AT HAYDOCK.

The single case of small-por which was promptly re- moved from flaydock to the temporary hospital on Newton Common, progregsing favourably, the worst stage having been passed. There has been no further outbreak, and unless it is imported from some infected district, there is no fear of any further cases.
THE OUTBREAK AT ST. HELENS. FURTHER HOSPITAL EXTENSION.

At the first monthly meeting of the Health Committee of the St. Helens Corporation, on Wednesday,Councillor J. Forster, who was re-elected as chairman, said there Lad unfortunate ly been an intreduction into St. Helens of smallpox. but he believed it had been arrested at its eommencement, and he felt sure that they were acting on the right lines and doing all they could to stamp it out. A great deat was due to the section of tie public who were fond of football,and they were extremely oblig- ed to them hr abandoning the match with Warrington. In fact, the whole Oahe public had assisted the medical officers in trying to, stop the spread of the disease.—A special report was read, which stated On October I 31 and November 1. the occurrence of six cases of small- pox came to our knowledge, one in Russell-st. and the others in Thatto Heath. The infection in all these was from the same source. All were removed to the, hospital. On Monday and Tuesday nine fresh cases were discovered at Thatto Heath, each of these having been infected by one or more of the previous six. All of the 16 cases were at once removed to the hospital with one, exception. The exceptional case was that of a man who. in the centre of a row of cottages,and who refuses to go to the hospital. On ascertaining this,' at once applied, under Section 124.,0f.the Public Health Act,and obtained last night a magistrate's order requiring his re- moval. So far this order has not been complied with.. The hospital was cleared of the convalescent scarlet fever cases, and at once got ready for the smallpox patients. It is just possible to.. get sixteen patients into the hospital, provided the sexes, correspond in number with the ward accommo- dation. As there was a very great probability of, secondary cases occurring, I recommended a wooden extension of the present building to hold twelve beds., At a special meeting of this Committee on Friday, the, 4th inst., this recommendation was passed,, and the building is now nearly furnished. By Friday night it, will be ready to receive cases. A visit was made to the. infected district every day, with the object of' learning of the existence of fresh cases. There is a probabilibr of only a few further cases occurring, but this is by. • means certain. The only way of efficiently stami out smallpox is by isolation at once. Delay in .isolation is extremely dangerous. I would, therefore;, recommend that the Committee grant instructions- to still further increase the hospital accommodation by the ' addition of another double ward exactly similar, tothe one that is now being put up, and this should be pro- ceeded with if thought necessary." lteferringto the case of the man who refused to., go to, the hospital,, the Town Clerksaid it would be as well;t• make it known that every patient suffering from small pox could be forcibly taken to the hospital, and if any- one obstructed them in so doing they were liakle to a penalty of BW. The man also rendered himself liableto. a penalty for not going. Alderman Gamble, C. 8.. asked if the man would be taken to the hospital to-day, under the magistrate's order. Dr. Robertson replied that he would, and stated that they had accommodation for sixteen patients in the main building, and the wooden erection would hold twelve more. They had now fifteen cases. He urged that another wooden building should be put up. The committee decided to do this, and instim.,— the medical. officers, if they found the existing build- ings were filling, to at ence put up another wooden building.

Brighouse, Coroner, held an inquest at the Bull's Head Inn, Lowton 'Junction, on the body of an 41 man named Edward Burrows, 65 'years of age, ot 29, Grant-st., Golborne, who committed suicide, by drowning himself in the Boundary brook at Golborne Dale, Newton, on Monday. It appears. the deceased who had been in failing health for the past 12 months, had been out of work for about four months, was attended by Dr. Dobb of Golborne. On Monday morning he left his bed at 7.30. and went out in the direction of the Boundary brook,which separates the townships of Lowton and Golborne, and was noticed to be loitering about the place. At 8.50 a man named Duddle was passing, and he observed a ca‘p and coat on the bank close to the bridge, and on a further examination he saw the body of a:man floating in tfie water. With the assistance of another man, the body was got out, life Wag then extinct, and it was removed to the Bull'a tread Inn. OUT WITH' THE POLICE COURT MISSIONARY.

it was in the Borough Police Court, the other week. The room was dull and gloomy: the grey, damp, murky light outside scarcely penetrated within the windows. An eighteen year old girl had just been tried for drunkenness, and, upon promising to accompany the Police Court Mission- ary, Mr. Taylor, to a home in Liverpool, she had been discharged. The writer had arranged to ac- company Mr. Taylor through the arduous rounds of duties which he performs in his capacity of Court Missionary. Before taking charge of the girl Mr. Taylor paid his usual visit to the cells. There was a large number of prisoners this morn- ing, both male and female, all waiting to he con- veyed to Walton or Strange ways jail. The men were 14uddled together in one cell. It was a small square stone department, with a plank bed at one end of the room, and a fire surr3unded with a strong iron guard at the other. The men lounged about the fire place, gazing moodily into the bright, dancing flames. No one spoke or noticedius as we entered, and they stood there a ragged, dirty crowd, a throng of hopeless, fallen men, of social outcasts ; a picture of the epitome of poverty, vice, drunkenness, cruelty, and immorality. There was only one amongst them who showed a sign of any- thing but impenetrable torpor and stupidity.. And, this one was a youth, who

SAT ON THE WOODEN RIM. crying. We found that "ss. and costs or 14 days" had been inflicted upon him for drunkenness. He had never been in jail before, and the prospect of the incar- ceration appeared to have unmanned him. When asked what his offence was, he made the answer which characterizes all the prisoners, and it was " Nothin'.". For some time he stoutly contended that he had been locked up and convicted for nothing whatever, but in a while he admitted that he had taken "too much." A. lengthy conversation ended in the youth signing the pledge, and Mr. Taylor securing sufficient money to pay the fine with. After procuring the names of others of , the prisoners who had been convicted for drunkenness, we proceeded to the female cell. A scene equally as pitiful as the one described,, presented itself. The women seemed friehtful in their blatant scoffing, and as Mr. Taylor led e'..t the girl whom he had taken under his charge, cruel and sarcastic cries of " make a Sunday school teacher on her," came from all quarters. The ridicule went home to the poor girl, and she left the cell with that half-ashanied air which is often observable in a person passing under a fire of contumely from one rank to another. Hers was a sad story. When 16 years of ago, a fair-haired fresh-complexioned, and lively girl, she succumbed to bad companionship and evil , passions. Her parents. both hardworking people, live in Town's End. Her wild and dissolute behaviour on one occasion gored her father on to passion, and one dark winter's night he turned her from his door—denied her his roof and sent her into the world,. an outcast ! From that time until this particular day she had associated with the worst female characters in the town, earning her livelihood by her own infamy,, selling herself for money and drink. BACK TO HER FATHER'S TIMM. Click I clack ! resounded her clogs on the pavement. We had left the police station now, the girl's face brightened and she turned to Mr. Taylor said : "I'm glad you offered to take me, sir, for IJ was never in jail before."—We proceeded with her to a lodging-house, a den which is known by the police to be the home of almost all the ill-famed women of the town, and which they cannot interfere with because of the restraining powers of a technicality in our laws. From the girl we gathered that there were at least 20)females who lived in that house, and not one of them was disassoci- ated with a criminal fashion of living. Now," said Mr. Taylor, " have you got all your clathes 2" "Yes," showing a small bundle. " Well, then, come and see your father before you go away." She shook her head, muttered something about being ashamed,and never, never, seeing him again. But in a while she was persuaded to "go and have just a look at him." And so we tramped off through the streets with her, the clatter of her unfortunate clogs bringing down a, considerable amount lf attention upon us as we proceeded past Market Gate and down Horsemarket-st. In about ten minutes we arrived at a workshop. The girl was rather pale now, her hands twitched nervously. A boy had gone to bring the father. In a few moments a tall grey- haired man came out, with his arms bare, and a leather apron on. He had never seen his daughter for two years ! He tnined to Mr. Taylor, and tried not to notice her; he was agitated. He put on a frown, and gruffly asked "Well rand Mr. Taylor began to explain, and the man sometimes turned his head away, fumbled with his eyes, and muttered something about dust or flies. In a few moments the trembling voice of the girl said, " Father.' The old man broke. The tears rolled fast and thick down his cheeks, and he sobbed like a child. The girl broke into a bitter outburst of tears) and ap- proaching him pleaded, "Forgive me father. Let me stop with you, and I'll mend." But these scenes are painful. Suffice it to say, the girl went home with her father, and n•w constitutes an instance of the benefit of timely interference and help. She was one of the worst, most hopeless, and pitiable classes of women that live, and a very great number of whom Mr. Taylor-says War• rington is pestered with.

div.head: TRACE OF TEN DRINK DIDION.
div.p: A TRACE OF TEN DRINK DIDION.

"The next case is about one of the most difficult cases of drunkenness I ever dealt with. It is a man who lost his wife the other month, but who has been drinking almost night and day since." We reached the house presently and knocked; the sound resounded hollowly in the lobby, but no sound else was heard. Another ran- tan! tan I' No answer. So Mr. Taylor tried, the door, found it unlocked, and we walked in. The room was almost bare of furniture. A strongly-built man sat at the table with a bottle of bear before him, and his head buried in his hands. He raised himself nervously when we entered, and hie hands trembled violently. After a few preliminaries, Mt. Taylor asked the man what he did with the beer there,since he promised the day before to keep the pledge. Why didn't he leave- the drink alone?. "Oh, God ! I wish I could leave it,.but I carn't. No, no, no, I carn't, I should die." He spoke almost deliriously. "Listen, hark! Don't you hear it moving in the next room?' He paused again, and his blood- shot eyes rolled. Then he craned over the table to us, and in a low husky voice, said, ' It's her ghost. I always hear it in that room when I'm by myself, and then I have to drink, drink, drink, until m happy." For some minutes the man ran on in this way, some- times denouncing the drink and in almost the same breath hugging the bottle to him with hysterical affec- tion. Mr. Taylor had a long talk with him, and when ' we left the poor fellow was infinitely calmer, especially when he heard that Mr. Taylor had found sufficient influence to have him reinstated in a situation he had I lost. This ca-e and the other one are fair exaraples of the difficult patients which the police court missionary has daily to contend with. WB YISITWD MANY OTLIBR "CAWS," and then commenced a search for a man who had promised to sign the pledge. It was off Fennel-st. We hunted about but couldn't meet with success for a time. Then we collided with our quest ithis se anner. We knocked at a door and a woman and a child came. Mr. Taylor said " Does Mr.—live here ?" " Well, begorra-oi-oi-oi dunno." " Come you must—" "Oh, 'ave course, per lordships ; he'l pay when he git the money." Then in a hurried whisper to the girl " run vs little imp and tell ye father the clubman's here." " No I'm not—"" Arra, d'ye think to catch Bridget shin- ing wid her eyes closed."" I'm not the clubman!" "Yar P " I'm not. I'm the Police Court Missionary." "And who the devil's that ?" Your husband's going to sign the pledge with me." " Musha t yet the blessed saviour of me Mike! Oh, an' didn't he swallow beer like al pumping engine till he met ye, may the Lorrard pre- serve a chair for ye in heaven—wait !" In a moment or two Mike was brought to the front by his wife. The portion of a fine paid for him by Mr. Taylor had done the work. He had been a teetotaller tor a week, and now signed the pledge. This was an instance of the difficulties which the Police Court Missionary contends. with in gaining first access to people whom he has met as defendants at the police court. One phase of his duties. consists of getting work for destitute men, at the Fire. wood Factory in Cedar-street, Liverpool, which the Church of England Liverpool Diocesan Police Court and Prison Gate Mission, are running. The missionary's work here is by no means light or devoid of responsibi- lity. Indeed from the following facts which he handed me, he appears to have very little time to exemplify the old saying that "idle fingers work mischief. These are the facts of his work for October.:— Total conversed with in courts and bridewell, 79 ; pledges taken, 33; cases visited from court, 117; men sent to Firewood Factory, 3; sent back to parents, 1; restored to parents or friends. 1 ; letters written re cases, 3; loss of employment averted by Missionary, 3; cases at- tended to by request of magistrates, 9; sent to other missionaries, 1; to other societies and clergy, 18 ; visits to lodging-houses, cab stands,&c.,4 ; men spoken to, 12 ; tracts distributed, 200; meetings addressed, 5; number of visits to courts, 33. seXU‘i le-

Ontrtion Sabbresoto. To THE ELECTORS OF' WEST DANK WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, It was my e•rnest de.ire to have been one- of the first elected Councillors to represent your Ward. but as the con- test developed I conceived it to be for the interests of the electors that I should withdraw in favour of a man of more experience than myself. One of your representatives having been made an Alder- man, I no beg to offer myself as an INDEPENDEWF CANDIDATE for your suffrages at this bye-eleation. If elec ed, I shall doall in my power to improve the general sanitary condition of the Town, knowing this to be most important for the Health of the Inhabitants; to keep up the present high efficiency of the Gas and Water undertakings with due economy ; to see that the streets are well lighted, and to do all in my power to increase the welfare of the Town, especially West Bank Ward. I am your obedient servant, WILLIAM WINWOOD GOSSAGB.

BOR °DO ii OF WIDNES ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF VICTORIA WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been nominated by representative and influential Burgesses In your Ward, I willingly place my services at your disposal. . I have resided and been an occupier in your Ward for snore than a quarter of a centdry, and know something of its requirements. . I eanconfldently appeal to my past services on the late Local Board, where I have acted for what I believe to be the true interests of the town, and some credit has been awarded me for the very prosperous condition ef the Gas and Water undertakings, and if you do me the honour to return me as one of your representatives, the same principles on which I have acted hitherto will guide me in the future, as I come before you independent of any political party. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedient servant, 11" • • BEN JA.MIN BROWN.

[' BOROUGH OF WIDNES ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST BANK WARD. LADIAS ANI? GENTLEMEN,— I have felt honoured in being chosen by my fellow-towns. men to serve them On the Local Board for so many years in the past (my first election being In 1873), and claim to have discharged my trust conscientiously, and am persuaded that all my actions have met with yore approval ; a fact which gives nie Inuit („T.;;;;;:ragement in Neponding to the hearty invitation extended to me by the ratepayers of West Bank Ward to come forward as a candidate for election to the • Municipal Council. : As a representative of large interests in the town. I am deeply and earnestly concerned in all matters affecting Its welfare. The roads have been placed in a very fair state of efficiency, and very many of the streets which were a disgrace to us have been sewered, made, and lighted at a reasonable cost to the property owners, whareby geod value has been obtained ; anti, whilst I am in favour of continuing this policy in the immediate future, I pledge myself that, if elected, I will keep a vigilant eye on the spending department of the Council, and will especially watch the interests of this im- portant Ward by doing all in my power to further any pro- ject which in my judgment will advance the comfort and welfare of the inhabitants. I am. Ladies and gentlemen. Your faithful and obedient servant, JOSHUA MIDWOOD.

WARRINGTON• VACCINATION The only certiin protection from Small-pox is vaccination and re-vaccination. This advice, reiterated time after time since the outbreak of the present epidemic, and by all kinds of methods pro- claimed to the people of Warrington, has this week been endorsed by the medical men of the town, who, at a large representative meeting, resolved : "That it is the unanimous opinion of this meeting that vaccination and re-vaccination remain the best po sible methods of stam ring out the present epidemic." At their request. the Health Committee of the Borough has taken upon itself the provision of gratuitous daily vaccination, and I have ceordingly made arrangements for carrying this out at the following places, where medical men of the town Will attend at Seven o'clock in the evening, beginning on Monday next:— WORKMEN'S CLUB. JOHN-STREET • OFFICE OF SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER, BANK PARK; and three other places for which the arrangements are not . yet complete, but which will be announced on the walls by placard. By order of the Health Committee, JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health
